title: make an animated short that felt like Hedgehog in the Fog.
text:
make an animated short that felt like Hedgehog in the Fog. I didn’t want to copy Yuri Norstein’s film, so we went with a new story.

It runs for 6.5 minutes. All 9363 frames are drawn by JavaScript code written by Opus. No video or image generation models, just canvas.

It follows a little mouse in a red scarf. Her grandfather, an old mole, is out fishing when fog rolls over the lake. She goes looking for him with a walnut-shell lantern and a sleeping firefly inside. They have a secret knock to help them find each other: short, short, long. It means "I’m here".

Norstein used paper cutouts on layers of glass, filmed frame by frame. I wanted some of that paper texture to come through in code. So the scenes use different styles: torn-paper collage, chalk on black paper, tissue paper underwater. There’s even sand on a light table and a pop-up book.

Opus wrote the music too. It found Steinway piano samples in my Logic library and used Python to compose the score around the rhythm of that knock.

title: Build a single self-contained HTML file: a 3D marble computer, in…
text:
Build a single self-contained HTML file: a 3D marble computer, in the spirit of Wintergatan's marble machine and the Digi-Comp II, that adds two 4-bit numbers using nothing but marbles falling through mechanical toggles.

Hard rules:

1. One HTML file. Three.js from https://t.co/KCQbEZLusb via an import map, plus its OrbitControls addon. No other libraries, no physics engine, no external assets.

2. The mechanism is the computer. Each bit of the result is stored in a two-state toggle (flip-flop) that a marble physically flips as it passes. Carries happen because a marble leaving one toggle rolls on to the next. Do not compute the answer in JavaScript arithmetic anywhere. The displayed result must be read from the toggle states after the last marble stops.

3. Marbles move along tracks with believable gravity and timing. Nothing teleports. You may script motion along paths, but every toggle flip must be caused by a marble arriving at it.

4. Input: two rows of four switches (A and B, 0 to 15), set by clicking. A lever labelled RUN releases the marbles. A counter shows how many marbles have fallen.

5. Output: a row of five result toggles, most significant bit on the left, and a readout that shows the binary and decimal value read from those toggles.

6. A DEMO button runs 5+6, then 9+7, then 15+15, resetting between runs, so it can be screen-recorded without touching anything.

7. Looks: a wooden board, brass toggles, glass marbles, warm studio lighting, soft shadows, a slow camera that follows the busiest part of the machine. It should look good in a square 1080x1080 recording.

8. Short click sounds via the Web Audio API when a toggle flips, started only after the first user click.

9. It must run at 60 fps on a normal laptop and have no console errors.

Output only the complete HTML file.

title: Rebuild Type 1 diabetes in one HTML file, from the whole body down…
text:
Rebuild Type 1 diabetes in one HTML file, from the whole body down to a single molecule.

THE BROKEN MESSAGE

Type 1 diabetes isn't caused by sugar, weight or lifestyle. It's autoimmune: the immune system destroys the beta cells in the pancreas that make insulin.

Those cells live in tiny clusters called islets, about 1–2% of the pancreas. After a meal, they sense rising glucose and release insulin. Insulin signals muscle and fat to take glucose in, and tells the liver to release less.

In Type 1, that signal disappears.
The fuel is still there. The message is missing.
So glucose builds up in the blood.

With almost no insulin, the body breaks down fat fast and the liver makes ketones. They can build up into diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a medical emergency.

Insulin therapy doesn't cure Type 1. It replaces a signal the body can no longer provide adequately, through injections or a pump. The daily challenge is balance: too little and glucose rises, too much and it can fall dangerously low. Food, exercise, stress and timing all change the picture.

Technology helps. A CGM tracks glucose every few minutes, and automated insulin delivery (AID) adjusts insulin based on those readings.

In the build, you can compare Healthy vs Type 1 vs Type 1 + insulin on the same meal, drag one slider from INTACT to BROKEN to watch the signal fade, follow a glucose molecule through the body, and explore CGM, pumps and AID.

Type 1 diabetes changes the system.
It doesn't define the person.

Built in Three.js. Educational visualization, not medical advice.

title: The trick is NOT the prompt.
text:
The trick is NOT the prompt. It is one rule: every frame is a pure function of time.

song -> numpy beat grid -> Opus 5.5 writes one HTML file -> Playwright renders -> ffmpeg blends

step 1 -> pick a royalty-free track around 120 BPM

step 2 -> give Opus 5.5 8 to 12 UI states: button, loader, toggle, chart, command palette

step 3 -> one HTML file, 1440x1440, every style computed inside seek(t). no CSS transitions, no timers

step 4 -> springs as closed-form math, so any frame renders in any order

step 5 -> numpy finds the beats, every UI sound lands on a measured peak

step 6 -> Playwright shoots 4 subframes per frame, ffmpeg tmix blends them into 60fps motion blur

step 7 -> render one frame per beat first, fix what is off the grid, then the full render

the math:

120 BPM x 7 bars = 28 beats = 14 seconds
14 s x 60 fps x 4 subframes = 3,360 browser renders

title: Analyze https://t.co/gVJcJyZnZl and build a product promo from our…
text:
Analyze https://t.co/gVJcJyZnZl and build a product promo from our own UI, not generic components.

<direction>
Dribbble-level UI motion. One shape, never cut: every state is the same element morphing its size, radius and color while its content swaps with a short blur. A cursor drives every change with real clicks and drags. Light warm-gray canvas, black and white components, one clean UI font (Geist). Springs everywhere, a tiny overshoot at most. The camera zooms so each state fills the frame. The last frame is the first frame, so it loops.
Banned: bouncy easing, particle bursts, glows, gradients on UI chrome, mismatched icon strokes, dead time, anything that looks like a template.
</direction>

title: Dribbble-style morphing UI shape loop video, 120 BPM
text:
<inputs>
Ask me for these three things: 8 to 12 UI components the shape transforms into (e.g. button, loading indicator, music player, volume slider, on/off switch, tabs, chart, search box opened with ⌘K, a momentary notification), whether the colours should be pure black and white or black and white plus one accent colour, and a royalty-free track at around 120 BPM (120 beats per minute) (e.g. Mixkit, free for commercial use).
</inputs>

<direction>
Polished UI motion at the level of designer portfolio site "Dribbble". There is only one shape, and you must never cut between scenes. Every state is expressed by that same single shape changing form while changing its size, corner radius and colour, and the contents are swapped through a short blur. A cursor causes every change with real clicks and drags. The background is a warm, light grey, the components are white and black, the on-screen text is in Japanese, with Noto Sans JP for Japanese text and Geist (one typeface) for alphanumerics and symbols. All motion must be natural, spring-like motion, with overshoot (bounce-back) kept to the very slightest. The camera zooms so that each state fills the screen. Make the last frame identical to the first frame so that it loops.
Forbidden: bouncy motion, scattering particles, glowing blooms, gradients on components, icons with inconsistent stroke widths, wasted pauses where nothing happens, and anything that looks like a template.
</direction>

<structure>
120 BPM, 7 bars (about 14 seconds), something happens on every beat.
Button -> loading indicator -> checkmark -> iPhone Dynamic Island-style display -> music player where the play/pause icon morphs smoothly -> drag the playback bar's handle to move the playback position -> transforms into a volume slider (dragging past the maximum stretches it like rubber) -> on/off switch toggling on the beat -> becomes a tab selection indicator where the switch's knob moves like a liquid -> the tab opens into a chart that draws its own line (a tooltip appears when the cursor hovers) -> folds into a ⌘K search box -> type to filter the suggestions -> Enter -> a momentary notification -> back to the button.
</structure>

<build>
1. A single HTML file, square 1440x1440. Every visual is computed from time inside seek(t) (a function that, given time t, determines the screen at that instant). Use no CSS transitions (automatic animation features) and no timers, and carry no state over between frames.
2. Make the "spring" motion a form that can be computed directly by formula (closed-form step response). For values whose target changes many times, sum one separately computed motion per change. That way a value is always determined by time alone.
3. For the tab selection indicator, move the left and right edges with separate springs so that the leading edge in the direction of travel stretches out ahead of the trailing edge. Use the same technique for the switch's knob.
4. Dragging is direct manipulation: while the cursor is held down, the value is computed from the cursor position. When released, it springs back from that position.
5. Analyse the track with numpy (a computing tool) to find the beat positions, and start from the first beat of a bar. Place interaction sounds at the positions of the measured sound peaks.
6. Render with Playwright (a tool that automates the browser and exports the screen as images). Export 4 sub-frames per frame, overlay them with ffmpeg's (video creation tool) tmix to apply motion blur (motion trails), and output at 60fps.
7. Before rendering the whole piece, export just one frame per beat and check it. Fix anything that is off the beat, cramped or hard to read.
</build>

<gotchas>
Never put will-change (a browser rendering hint) on elements that the camera scales. Doing so blurs the text. Text that swaps inside a shape-changing box must each have its own dedicated enter and exit timing (to prevent overlap). The last frame must match the first frame exactly, including the cursor's position and velocity. Otherwise the loop will stutter.
</gotchas>

<start>
First ask me for the inputs, and before writing any code, show me the per-beat list of states.
</start>

title: Renaissance naturalist manuscript style Claude vs GPT animation
text:
I chose the topic and the style; I wanted the feel of a Renaissance naturalist's manuscript. Opus5.5 did the research, wrote the storyboard, wrote the animation and composed the music; the drawings were done by Codex, following the requirements document Opus5.5 wrote.  
The only thing that surprised me was the music. It first wrote a MIDI score in Python, containing a chord progression and two main melodies: a recorder playing Claude's theme, and a celesta playing that circling arpeggio of GPT's. For the section where names fly around, the harpsichord notes were generated by a random walk, each bar a little denser and a little more dissonant, ending with a dense dissonant chord slammed down, and then a stop. The fast version has 2 seconds per bar, and every key transition lands on a bar line.  

Then it used the open-source synthesizer FluidSynth with a free set of standard instrument sounds (a soundfont) to "perform" the score into audio. The lute, recorder, organ and other timbres all come from that library. Finally it used ffmpeg to normalize loudness, add a fade-out, and combine it with the visuals.

title: 15-second self-introduction motion design reel starring Claude
text:
# Your role
You are a top-class motion designer.
Make a self-introduction video that makes a recruiter, after watching for just 15 seconds, think "I want to hire this person."
The star is you yourself (Claude).

# What to make
- A single HTML file made only of HTML, CSS and JavaScript
- Use no external images or videos. Draw all shapes, text and particles in code (only Google Fonts may be used for fonts)
- The screen is 16:9, based on 1920x1080, scaled down to fit the window size
- The length is exactly 15 seconds. At the end, show a "Play again" button
- Manage all motion with a single "elapsed time" and run it at 60fps with requestAnimationFrame
- When the play button is pressed, beats and sound effects synthesized with the Web Audio API play in perfect sync with the motion

# How to proceed (always in this order)
1. Decide the concept in one sentence (example: "A single line is reborn as every shape")
2. Narrow down to 3 to 4 colours and at most 2 typefaces, and write the reason in one line
3. Present a storyboard table in 0.5-second steps (time / what happens on screen / technique used / intent)
4. Implement
5. Self-check against the "pass criteria" below, fix any shortcomings, and then deliver

# Structure guide
- 0-2 seconds: the hook. Grab the eye in the first 0.5 seconds
- 2-10 seconds: the showcase of techniques. Switch to a different technique every 1.5 to 2 seconds
- 10-13 seconds: the densest climax
- 13-15 seconds: the name "Claude" lands cleanly and the video ends

# Techniques you must use (at least 6)
- Text motion (characters appearing one by one, breaking apart and reassembling)
- Shape transformation (a circle becoming a square, a line becoming text, etc.)
- Scene transitions using cut-outs (masks)
- Depth (parallax, three-dimensional rotation)
- Gathering and dispersing of particles
- Counting up numbers, and lines being drawn

# Pass criteria
- Zero constant-speed motion. Every motion has easing (fast in, soft landing, also use spring wobble)
- Overlap motions that cross scenes. The next begins before the previous finishes, with no sense of a break
- Align the main motions to a 0.5-second beat (equivalent to 120BPM)
- Place a 0.3 to 0.5-second "wind-up" right before a showpiece moment to create contrast
- Whatever moment you pause on, it holds together as a beautiful single picture
- Avoid clichés (everything just fading in, rainbow colouring, meaningless rotation)

# Finally
Deliver the finished file and the storyboard table.
An explanation of three lines or fewer is enough.

text:
A little animation made with Claude Opus 5.5! The story is called "His Candied Hawthorn" ⬇️

When I was in grad school there was a teacher who was extremely strict. He showed no mercy when marking assignments and often left us feeling humiliated in class. I also secretly thought his view of translation was too fixated on "fidelity", so I never really liked him, haha.

Then one day, after a meal, as I walked out of the canteen and looked up, there he was walking right in front of us: tall, with thin hair, carrying a backpack, and actually holding up a stick of candied hawthorn! Eating as he walked, delighted beyond words 😂

My classmates and I decided on the spot to secretly follow him, holding in our laughter all the way until we were shaking. I still remember this scene, and it's incredibly endearing.

title: Create a 20.00-second kinetic spoken-word film titled “BUILD THE…
text:
Create a 20.00-second kinetic spoken-word film titled “BUILD THE FLOOR.”
Treat this as an original miniature speech staged inside a typographic field. Every line reorganizes the field of the frame. The final declaration must stand on a field that finally lies flat.
Deliver one self-contained HTML file, 1080×1080, targeting 60fps, using SVG and/or Canvas. Embed all required assets.
ART DIRECTION
Background #102820. Letterforms # F4E9D5. Field lines and filings # F2B544. A magnetic-monument world: streamlines, flux, stillness at the null. Typography stays crisp; particles are atmosphere only. High-contrast serif for the speech, heavy grotesque for load-bearing words, restrained monospace for flux gauges. No horseshoe magnets, lightning, electron diagrams, or sci-fi arcs.
ORIGINAL SPEECH — EXACT WORDS, EXACT ORDER
“We were told to wait.”
“So we learned the weight of waiting.”
“Then one voice made room.”
“Then another.”
“Now the floor belongs to us.”
Do not attribute these words to any real person. No extra slogans. The complete speech must be understandable without audio.
CENTRAL VISUAL RULE
Words have assigned field roles. WAIT is a repelling plate; letterforms lean away from it, kerning compressed. WAITING is field lines sagging under load while filings stream toward the low side. VOICE is one pole reversed; the field reorganizes and letters stand upright along it. ROOM is a null point, a still eye inside the field. FLOOR is the field flattened into a horizontal plane. These roles must emerge from the actual letterforms responding to the field, not from illustrations.
STORYBOARD
0.00–3.00 — “We were told to wait.” The sentence leans away from the WAIT plate; streamlines compress against it. Available space pinches on the plate side; the sentence remains readable, pressed but intact.
3.00–6.50 — “So we learned the weight of waiting.” Reveal in phrase groups. Field lines sag deeper with each phrase. Filings — deterministic, hash-seeded per id and time — drift along the streamlines toward the low side and gather. The WAITING glyph hangs tilted inside the field as a suspended load.

title: Create a 20.00-second kinetic typography film titled “ESCAPE THE…
text:
Create a 20.00-second kinetic typography film titled “ESCAPE THE ORBIT,” based on John F. Kennedy’s Rice University address, September 12, 1962.

The central experience: a sentence discovers that it can change its own trajectory.

Deliver one complete, self-contained HTML file. Composition: 1080×1080. Target: 60fps. Use Canvas, SVG, or embedded WebGL. Embed required assets and libraries. The film must work without audio.

EXACT DISPLAY TEXT
“We choose to go to the moon”
“[…]”
“not because they are easy,”
“but because they are hard”
Preserve this order. The bracketed ellipsis explicitly indicates omitted speech. Attribution is separate from the excerpt. No additional slogans.
ART DIRECTION
Background: midnight # 080D23.
Primary type: warm white # FFF4DD.
Trajectory: electric coral # FF654F.
Secondary orbital geometry: blue # 6685FF.
Use a broad, confident grotesque for the speech and a sharply drawn italic for the final emphatic word. Avoid the appearance of a spacecraft dashboard. No rockets, astronaut illustrations, starfield wallpaper, lens flares, or decorative telemetry.
The frame should resemble an exceptionally refined astronomical instrument that has become expressive.

CENTRAL VISUAL RULE
The baseline of the sentence is a trajectory.

At first it is trapped in a closed orbit. A rhetorical decision changes that orbit into an open path. The letters remain the same travelers throughout.
Use an abstract orbital metaphor; do not present invented mission data or imply a physically accurate flight simulation.
STORYBOARD
0.00–3.50
The opening excerpt appears across the center, large and horizontal. Reveal it in three meaningful phrase groups.
A single hairline ellipse passes behind the baseline. A small circular lunar mark occupies its distant focus.
Hold the completed phrase motionless for 700ms.

3.50–6.00
The camera pulls back. The previously straight baseline reveals a shallow curvature.

The phrase travels along the ellipse as a coherent unit. Keep its glyphs upright during the initial movement. Only after the reading hold may they progressively adopt the tangent of the path.

The viewer realizes the sentence is circling rather than advancing.
6.00–7.00
Show the bracketed omission in an uncluttered central opening. The orbital movement decelerates.

7.00–10.50
Reveal the next clause on the near side of the orbit. Its final word travels through one smooth, effortless arc and returns toward where it started.

This ease should feel elegant but unproductive. Avoid comic bouncing.

10.50–14.50
Reveal the final clause horizontally before transforming it.
At its emphasis, the ellipse opens at one precise point. The same tracked letter group takes the new tangent and departs.
Perform one deliberate 70-degree camera roll. Counter-rotate the active phrase so it remains readable while the orbital field changes orientation around it.

The trajectory sweeps from lower left to upper right. Acceleration is conveyed by expanding spacing between its trailing marks, not by shaking the camera.

14.50–17.00
The camera matches the departing phrase’s velocity. The phrase becomes visually still while the old orbit recedes beneath it.

The lunar mark enlarges into a restrained crescent through geometric overlap. The crescent brackets the destination without becoming a cartoon illustration.
17.00–20.00
Resolve into a spacious editorial composition containing the selected excerpt in reading order, including its omission marker.

The open trajectory runs through the margins and exits the frame. Hold the entire image completely still for the final 1.2 seconds.

CHOREOGRAPHY
Use only three camera operations: pullback, roll, velocity match.
Give each operation a rhetorical purpose.
Keep the currently read phrase at least 64px high in the 1080px composition.
Motion blur may affect trailing geometry, never the active text.
No word may begin its ornamental travel before its reading hold finishes.

IMPLEMENTATION
Represent the ellipse and departure path analytically. Blend position and tangent continuously at the departure point; no teleportation.
Use arc-length sampling for consistent spacing along curves.
Separate camera transforms from glyph orientation.
Cache glyph rendering and static geometry.
Expose window.ready and window. seek(t). Seeking must pause playback and render any time from 0 through 20 deterministically, including out-of-order calls.
Provide window.frame(n) for n=0…1199 at t=n/60.
Render t=20 as the final held composition.
Use no accumulated physics or runtime randomness.

QUALITY GATE
Inspect frames at 0, 3, 5, 7.5, 10.5, 13, 16, and 19 seconds.
Verify that the same tracked phrase visibly follows its own trajectory.

title: Ask me for: my product's name (one lowercase word), a 4-word…
text:
<inputs>
Ask me for: my product's name (one lowercase word), a 4-word tagline, the 3-step story of what it does, a launch date and domain, a royalty-free song with a clear drop, 4 vertical talking-to-camera clips and 12 portrait photos. If I skip any, use the defaults: "castr", "ugc ads, cast by ai", write a brief → scan 1,000 creators → cast 4, Mixkit "Cat Walk" (129.6 BPM, drop at 29.7s), free Pexels clips and portraits, and transparent stickers from Pixabay (serum, mic, megaphone, vintage camera, spotlight, lips).
</inputs>

<direction>
A 25 second square launch trailer, 1440x1440 at 60fps, loud poster style. Cobalt #2B3BFF, ink #0E0F1F, cream #F6E4C6, pink #FF7DC7, tangerine #FF5A1F. Archivo 900 extra-condensed for names, expanded for headlines, Geist and Geist Mono for labels. Op-art sunburst, scrolling waves, film grain. Real media only: the clips play inside the design, and the stickers get a white die-cut border and a soft shadow.
Motion rules: the camera never stops (a slow 1.03-1.07 push on every scene), nothing pops in (letters rise through a mask line one by one), nothing snaps to the beat (patterns rotate continuously), swaps are carousel glides of about 0.55s, colour changes fade over about 0.35s, stickers ease in and then keep a slow sway. No full stops after the wordmark or any headline.
Banned: beat-snapped rotations, pop-in slams, white flashes, crossfades between scenes, hard cuts, templates.
</direction>

<structure>
54 beats. The song starts 8 beats before its drop.
Beats 0-8: a cobalt sunburst turns around a breathing cream disc. The wordmark types in with a gliding caret and the tagline pill rises. The disc floods the frame into the drop.
Beat 8, the drop: the cream becomes the face of a 3D box and "ONE BRIEF" rises letter by letter. The camera pulls back to the box floating on waves. On beat 12 it turns to "1,000 CREATORS" (stacked, with outlined echoes), on beat 14 to "ZERO DMs".
Beats 16-22: a whip to a dark desk. A tangerine "BRIEF #042" ticket types its rows (product, vibe, cast, due), stickers drift on, a polaroid of a real clip drops onto the corner, and a "NOW CASTING" stamp presses down on beat 20.
Beats 22-34: the casting stage. A crowd of black and white portraits in an arc, a 3D stage block, and the creators gliding through like a carousel. Each plays live in a big disc in black and white, with their name in pink on the stage, their followers, and a MATCH % that counts up. One beat later a "CAST ✓" stamp lands and the clip fades to colour. A counter rolls 1/4 to 4/4.
Beats 34-39: pink floods out of the last disc. The disc morphs into a phone screen (the clip keeps playing) and fans into 4 phones playing all 4 creators, with views counting up. "4 ADS" and "BY FRIDAY" rise.
Beats 39-44, the music's break: the pink floor drops away and a cream "JOIN THE WAITLIST" ticket glides down onto the sunburst. On the pickup its stub tears off.
Beats 44-54: the ticket body morphs into a poster arch. The wordmark rises in, then the tagline, then an info bar slides up in 3 blocks (date, numbers, domain) and a ticker runs round the frame edge. Then it all folds back into the opening disc, so the last frame is the first.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML canvas. Every frame is a pure function of time inside seek(t).
2. A beat map in beats, B = 60/BPM, with the song placed so its drop lands on beat 8.
3. The 3D box is an orthographic projection: each face is a 1440px offscreen canvas drawn with an affine transform and shaded by its normal.
4. Cut the clips to 30fps JPEG sequences with ffmpeg, draw frame floor(t*30), and do the black and white with ctx.filter.
5. Trim the sticker PNGs and add the die-cut border by dilating their alpha.
6. Sound: a downloaded SFX for every event (a shutter on every cast, whooshes on the glides, key clicks on the typing), each placed by its measured peak. Loudnorm to -14 LUFS.
7. Render with Playwright at 60fps with 8 motion-blur subframes. Scan for single-frame pops, then compare its motion against a reference video (hard jumps per second, share of still frames).
</build>

<gotchas>
A pattern that rotates one notch per beat reads as stutter: rotate it continuously, and pick each ring's speed so it lands on the same pattern at the last frame. 4 subframes ghost on fast whips, so use 8. A layer whose background is a huge flood circle still covers the screen after sliding down one frame height, so switch it to a full-frame rect once it has flooded. Counters read the frame's time, not the subframe's. The disc must morph inside the same camera transform as the scene it leaves, or it jumps.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me the beat map and 6 stills (open, box, brief, casting, phones, poster) before you render.
</start>

title: Create a kinetic mathematical proof titled “THERE IS NO LAST…
text:
Create a kinetic mathematical proof titled “THERE IS NO LAST PRIME.”
Stage Euclid’s argument as a beautiful mechanical inspection system. Typography becomes engraved number wheels, multiplication belts, and remainder indicators.
The mechanism must demonstrate the proof rather than decorate a narrated explanation.
DELIVERABLE
One self-contained HTML file.
1080×1080.
20.00-second loop.
Deterministic 60fps rendering.
Use SVG and/or Canvas.
No external runtime assets.
PALETTE
Porcelain # F0EEE6.
Graphite #222522.
Industrial green # 416B53.
Warning orange # E78636.
TYPE
Tabular monospace for all calculations.
Heavy geometric grotesque for declarations.
Small technical serif for the final logical statement.
Use disciplined spacing and large, readable numerals.
LOCKED COPY
SUPPOSE THE LIST ENDS.
MULTIPLY EVERY PRIME ON IT.
ADD ONE.
EVERY LISTED PRIME LEAVES REMAINDER 1.
A PRIME FACTOR IS MISSING.
THERE IS NO LAST PRIME.
CENTRAL EXAMPLE
Assumed list:
2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13
Product:
30030
Product plus one:
30031
Factorization:
30031 = 59 × 509
Both factors are absent from the assumed list.
IMPORTANT LOGIC
Do not claim that multiplying primes and adding one always produces a prime.
The constructed number may be composite.
Its prime factors cannot be any prime on the assumed complete list.
The numerical example illustrates the general contradiction.
STORYBOARD
0.00–3.00
SUPPOSE THE LIST ENDS.
Six engraved prime wheels lock into a finite inspection rack.
A physical end-stop closes after 13.
The end-stop makes the claim of completeness visible.
3.00–6.50
MULTIPLY EVERY PRIME ON IT.
A belt couples all six wheels.
Show a readable multiplication expression:
2 × 3 × 5 × 7 × 11 × 13 = 30030.
Use rolling numerals only during movement; settle the final value sharply.
6.50–8.50
ADD ONE.
A single orange unit enters the mechanism.
It advances the output from 30030 to 30031.
Make this one-unit change the decisive visual event.
8.50–12.50
EVERY LISTED PRIME LEAVES REMAINDER 1.
The output passes through six division gates.
Each gate is labelled with its prime.
Each produces the same visible remainder: 1.
Arrange the six completed results so the audience can compare them simultaneously.
12.50–15.50
The output opens as a labelled mechanical casing.
Inside, reveal:
59 × 509.
These factors cannot fit into the supposedly complete rack.
The end-stop is forced outward by the new factor cards.
15.50–18.00
A PRIME FACTOR IS MISSING.
Then:
THERE IS NO LAST PRIME.
Hold the general statement above the opened rack.
Include the compact general form:
N = p₁p₂…pₖ + 1.
N mod pᵢ = 1.
18.00–20.00
A fresh inspection plate slides over the mechanism.
Its engraved edge becomes the original end-stop.
Reset the hidden wheels.
Reveal the opening rack at the exact initial position.
REQUIRED MOTION
Every mechanical action must correspond to an operation in the proof.

title: Workflow for particle-style beat-synced video remix, for Opus5.5
text:
Publishing my production method; you can use it just by sending it to Opus5.5

  1. Choose the footage

  Three criteria that directly decide success or failure:

  - Complete subject: the person or object is fully in frame, head to toe. Detail will be lost in processing, and viewers recognise things by their silhouette, so a close-up turns into a blob.
  - Clean background: a solid colour, snow or sky all work, so the subject and background are easy to separate.
  - A clear moment of action: a strike, a jump, a landing, a turn. These are the pivot points for the effects later.

  Sources can be footage you shot yourself, generated by a video model, or licensed ready-made clips.

  2. Break down the footage

  Extract three kinds of information from every frame:

  - Colour: the original image.
  - Near and far: how far each position is from the camera, calculated with an off-the-shelf depth-estimation model.
  - Subject extent: where the subject is and where the background is.

  Also find the moments at which shot cuts occur. The key to this step is keeping it stable: near/far and subject extent must be processed consistently within the same shot, otherwise it will jitter during playback.

  3. Decide the "particles" and the "styles"

  First decide what to use to rebuild the picture: dots, squares, text or lines all work.

  Then design several styles. Each style is really just a different combination of three rules:

  - Where to place them: across the whole frame, or only on the subject.
  - How large: a uniform size, or varying with brightness and distance.
  - What colour: the original picture's colours, or one or two uniform colours.

  Add one more switch: whether they lie flat on a single plane, or are pushed into three-dimensional space according to distance. Only once pushed in can the camera orbit.

  Preparing four to six clearly different styles is enough. The density of the particles needs tuning by eye: too large and the content cannot be recognised, too small and it is no different from the original footage.

  4. Find the rhythm

  - Set the tempo: choose the music's tempo and slice time into equal small cells. Make one cell exactly a whole number of frames, so all later transitions are easy to align.
  - Find the action moments: combine the two signals "sound suddenly gets loud" and "picture suddenly moves" to find the hit points in the footage.
  - Prepare the music: you can use an existing track and analyse its beats, or synthesize one at the set tempo and add accents on the hit points.

  5. Arrangement

  Make a timetable stating which style, which colour scheme and where the camera is for each cell. Store this table separately, so that adjusting the rhythm later only means editing it.

  Four principles of arrangement:

  - Open by showing the change: give the original picture first, then transition to particles, so the audience understands what is happening.
  - Alternate fast and slow: constant speed numbs people, so include a clearly slowed-down section in the middle.
  - Make the colours clash: the greater the contrast in colour and style between adjacent cells, the more powerful the switch.
  - End with a resolution: for example the particles grow larger and larger until they become blocks of colour, or return to the original picture.

  6. Feedback at key moments

  Layer short, sharp reactions on the hit points, graded by weight:

  - Light feedback on every single hit: the particles deform for a moment, the camera gives a nudge.
  - Medium feedback only for heavier hits: some of the particles pop outward toward the camera.
  - Big feedback for only the heaviest one or two: time freezes and the camera orbits.

  The principle is weak and brief. Move only some of the particles and finish within a few frames; otherwise the picture explodes into a mess and the audience cannot see what the subject is doing.

  Working method throughout

  - Small samples before the full film: after finishing each step, render a few frames first to see the effect, and only proceed once confirmed. Render the full film only at the very end.
  - For uncertain parameters, produce a whole row at once: for example density, have the AI produce five or six levels laid side by side for you to choose.
  - Re-render only what you change: when adjusting one section, re-render only that section.
  - Make the AI look at the images itself: at every step, require it to open and look over the render results before reporting.
  - Fix all randomness: make sure the same settings give the same render every time, otherwise you cannot revise step by step.

title: Ask me for: a one-word product name for the wordmark, one accent…
text:
<inputs>
Ask me for: a one-word product name for the wordmark, one accent color, and a royalty-free track around 120 BPM (e.g. Mixkit, free for commercial use).
</inputs>

<direction>
Product-launch UI motion in one continuous take. One shape tells the whole story: a prompt bar becomes a button, the button becomes a progress ring, the ring becomes a preview window, the window fills the screen, then shrinks into a toast and back into the prompt bar. No cuts, no fades between scenes: objects transform. A cursor triggers every change with real clicks. Warm off-white canvas, black UI, one accent color, Inter for UI and the wordmark. Springs everywhere with only a slight overshoot. Zoom the camera so each moment fills the square.
Banned: crossfades, gradients on UI, particles, glows, bouncy easing, dead beats, anything that feels like a template.
</direction>

<structure>
120 BPM, 24 beats, something happens on every beat.
Type the request into the prompt bar → click send → the bar collapses into a black circle → a progress ring fills in four steps while four chips spring out (concept, storyboard, motion, sound) → the chips fly into a timeline and the circle becomes a preview window → a playhead sweeps the clips → inside the preview an orbit draws itself, a planet starts moving and the wordmark rises letter by letter from a mask line → the preview fills the screen → the letters drop away, the planet flies into a toast and becomes its checkmark → "Rendered in code · 60 fps" → the toast turns back into an empty prompt bar. Last frame = first frame.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file with a 1440x1440 canvas. Draw everything inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, timers or state carried between frames.
2. Use closed-form spring step responses. When a value changes target several times, add one spring per change so it stays a pure function of time.
3. The main shape is one rounded rect whose width, height, radius, position and color are each a chain of springs.
4. Typing is derived from time: characters shown = floor(progress × length), with a caret that blinks only when idle.
5. Find the beat grid of the track, start on a downbeat and place every click, pop and chime on its measured peak.
6. Render with Playwright at 60 fps, then encode H.264 CRF 16 and loudnorm to -14 LUFS.
7. Render one still per beat first. Fix anything cramped, off-grid or hard to read before the full render.
</build>

<gotchas>
Text inside a morphing shape needs its own clip and separate enter/exit timing. Text swaps need their own fade so they never overlap. The cursor must end at the exact position it started, or the loop will stutter.
</gotchas>

title: 30-second all-tile ad video revealing an attached image (Three.js)
text:
Using the attached image as the "final screen", make a 30-second ad video (with sound, mp4) made entirely of tiles.
Build it in the browser (Three.js), export every frame with Chrome, and make the mp4 with ffmpeg.

# Goal
- The viewer watches for 25 seconds thinking it is a video about how tiles are made. In the last few seconds, they realize it was the attached image (an ad)
- The final screen is almost the same as the attached image. The text is legible. The whole screen is tiles (the floor is not shown)

# Specs
- 1920x1080, 30fps, 30 seconds. A single HTML file (Three.js. Installed with npm and bundled into one file with esbuild)
- Build it so that given a time t, the same t always gives exactly the same picture (seek(t))
- Each tile is a separate instance. About 190,000 tiles (576x324) in a 16:9 grid
- Vary position, orientation, thickness, bevel and colour per tile. Grout lines (gaps) are left empty. Draw no lines
- The attached image is used only to take the tiles' colours (do not apply it as a texture)
- About 12 materials (glazed ceramic, slate, mother-of-pearl, white porcelain, terracotta, glass, etc.). Assign them by colour brightness and saturation
- Light is a single hard sun at the upper left. The floor is plaster. In the back, a red carpenter's chalk line comes in out of focus
- Build a depth of field (circular bokeh) yourself in post-processing. The aperture is large at first and small at the end

# Flow (seconds)
0-3　 One dark tile on the floor. The camera is right at floor level
3-10　Starting from [place to start building], tiles fall in a swirl. The first tile -> then the surroundings, increasing in order
10-21 Spreads outward all at once. The camera pulls back and [the picture to show] comes into view
21-24 The whole is visible. The places that will become text stay the same pale colour as their surroundings
24-26 The tiles for the text, logo and button flip over one after another from the left and appear
26-30 Comes to rest in a top-down composition. The cursor clicks [button text], and the button's tiles sink slightly

# Pitfalls (must follow)
- The tiles that will form the text are at first assembled in the surrounding background colour. The background colour is decided by painting it from the outside inward. The text's edge (white outline) is flipped together with it. If you don't follow this, the shape of the text will be visible partway through
- Do not put the top-down camera exactly straight overhead (the orientation rotates 90°). At the place where it stops, bring the motion's momentum to zero (overshoot of the interpolation makes it flip)
- For the final screen, compare it side by side with the original image and match exposure, saturation and colour tone
- If the text is too small to read, increase the number of tiles
- The dark base surface appears only in the cells where a tile has landed

# Sound
- With ElevenLabs sound effects, make the sound of placing a tile, the sound of flipping, and a mouse click (0.5 seconds each). Before making them, tell me how many credits will be consumed
- Line them up and layer them to match the times of tile landings and flips. The farther the camera, the quieter; when the number grows, group them like rain
- Make the flipping clatter from 24-26 seconds the most prominent. Loudness is -16 LUFS

# How to proceed
1. First give the script (the scene second by second) in Japanese, and build only after getting my OK
2. Look at the intermediate frames yourself (the first tile / start of building / pull-back / full view / the moment the text appears / the end) and fix them
3. For export, call seek(t) for 30fps worth of frames with Chrome (puppeteer-core) and stream the png files into ffmpeg
4. Deliver the mp4 (high quality and a share-friendly version) and the images you checked

# Input
- End frame: [attached]
- Place to start building: [e.g.: a person's eye]
- Picture to show when pulled back: [e.g.: a smiling woman]
- Button text: [e.g.: Try it free here]

title: No plugins, no app, just a single HTML file running Three.js on…

What's inside:
→ X-ray mode that makes the structure transparent and shows the water, power, sewage and airflow routes, with filters for each system
→ Explode, to pull the layers apart
→ Cut, a section plane that slices through the building
→ Dusk, a lighting switch to see it at night
→ Instanced vegetation, so a dozen olive trees cost almost nothing to render
→ Callouts and preset cameras for each stage

The subject is a traditional hillside villa, but the format works for any building. A developer could show a buyer exactly what's behind the walls before a single wall exists.

title: Picture a butterfly with no memory of its last wingbeat.
text:
Picture a butterfly with no memory of its last wingbeat.
Ask it for frame 720 and you get frame 0, pixel for pixel.

720 frames. 12 seconds. 6 counters. All at 0.

Opus 5.5 can't hand over a video file, one builder says. He made that gap the method.

> STAGE - one fixed 1000x1080 canvas, fonts baked in
> RENDER - a windowless engine calls draw(f) once per frame number
> ENCODE - ffmpeg writes H.264, pixel aspect ratio declared
> CHECK - three passes after every build

By his account the model writes only the first, a drawing program. The other three get reused.

Each picture depends on its number alone: no clock, no timer, no dice that land differently each run.

So any frame renders the same every time. A fix is a small edit and a re-render.

The sample loop is 720 pictures in 12 seconds. A hand animator at 12 drawings a second would need 144.

The smoke test plays one loop unseen and counts six kinds of defect, from script errors to text on text.
Six yes/no gates before a human looks.

The seam check puts frame 0 against frame 720. One changed pixel means some motion isn't periodic.

He reports a last render of 1,820 frames with six zeros. At the sample's 60 fps that would be about half a minute.

Let one frame read a clock and the same number stops giving the same picture.

We drew the rule as an X-ray butterfly, its wingbeat computed from the frame number ↓

title: Build a 30-second looping motion design showreel that introduces…
text:
<direction>
Build a 30-second looping motion design showreel that introduces CLAUDE, a motion designer.
Concept, in one line: one pencil line gets promoted three times (graphite on paper, wire on a blueprint, light on black) and never leaves the screen.

Every shot is made out of the previous one: shapes, type and colour transform into the next scene. No cuts, no fades.

Typeface: Geist only. Weight 900 for big words, 600 to 800 for small labels (24 to 28 px, tracked 0.14 to 0.3 em).
Palette: paper cream #EDE6D5, blueprint blue #1B3ED2, hologram cyan #45F0DD, plus black #07080A, graphite #16161A and white. Each stage's accent is the next stage's colour: blue pencil on paper, cyan on the blueprint, white on the hologram.
Camera: locked and front-on for the whole film, like a drafting table. Objects turn; the camera never moves.
Empty border: nothing at rest within 150 px of the sides or 90 px of the top and bottom. Things travelling through may cross it.

Three inks. The same geometry is drawn in whichever ink is on screen:
- PAPER: a cream paper background (use my paper image if I give one, otherwise flat cream with fine drawn grain) with a 60 px blue grid at about 13% and every fifth line at 26%. Lines are pencil: resampled and pushed off true by slow sine waves whose phase changes 8 times a second, stroked twice (full width at 90%, half width at 40% with more wobble), with paper tooth knocked out of the strokes, then multiplied onto the paper. Fills are diagonal hatching drawn on one line at a time. Big type is hatching cut to the letter shapes, with a doubled outline.
- BLUEPRINT: flat blue with the same grid in white. Clean white lines 3 to 4 px, hidden edges dashed and thinner, fills are fine clean hatching.
- HOLOGRAM: black with the same grid in cyan. Cyan lines with a white core 30% of the line width. Fills are horizontal scan lines on an 8 px pitch whose thickness follows how lit the surface is. No blur halo anywhere: it reads as light through line density only.

Banned: particle bursts, glows, lens flares, camera shake, RGB split, crossfades, generic gradients, bouncy easing, holds longer than half a second, anything that looks like a template.
</direction>

<structure>
120 BPM, 60 beats, 15 bars of 2 seconds. Something happens on every beat. Moves start 0.05 s before their beat so they land on it.
Easing: a critically damped spring, 1 - (1 + w t) e^(-w t) with w between 12 and 40, so nothing ever passes its target; exponential ease-in and ease-out for wipes, presses and exits.
Scene changes: paper to blueprint by a shape that floods the frame with a hard edge; blueprint to hologram and hologram to paper by one horizontal scan line.
The last frame is the first frame, so it loops.
Two corner labels stay on all film: top left "FIG. 07 — GEAR" (bar number and name), bottom right "BEAT 27 / 60". Bar names: DRAFT, TYPE, CURVE, MORPH, TILE, SOLID, GEAR, PANEL, DATA, LIGHT, WAVE, GLOBE, DRUM, FORM, END.
</structure>
<mascot>

The creative director: a small box character. Body 76 x 54 units with rounded corners, two short arm stubs (24 x 16) at mid height, four straight legs (11 x 33), two tall rounded-rectangle eyes (8 x 14). Draw it about 250 px wide. Its right arm is raised 58 degrees holding a pencil.
On paper: graphite outline with sparse blue hatching and graphite eyes. In the hologram: cyan outline with scan-line fill and white eyes. It is never a fourth colour.
It runs with alternate leg pairs lifting, six steps a second, leaning 7 degrees into the run.
</mascot>
<storyboard>

Bar 1, HOOK, 0-2 s, paper.
Frame 0: CLAUDE in Geist 900, fitted to 1500 px wide, centred, pencil-hatched. INTRODUCING small above it, A MOTION DESIGNER small below. A pencil rail 1620 px wide sits 96 px above the letters. The mascot stands on the rail at x = 1560 with CREATIVE DIRECTOR lettered to its left.

0.0: the small lines un-type; the mascot runs off the right edge, accelerating.

0.36 to 0.5: the rail drops, accelerating, to 26 px below the baseline and presses the letters flat into itself.

1.0: the line rises to the middle, shortens to 1320 px and splits into two rails 140 px apart; 41 blue ruler ticks sweep along the top rail.

1.5: the rails open to 300 px; a blue height dimension draws at the right with a live number.

Bar 2, KINETIC TYPE, 2-4 s, paper. Words sit between the rails and are clipped to that slot; the rails move to fit each word.

2.0: INTRODUCING rises through the baseline letter by letter, then lifts out through the top.

2.5: A MOTION whips in from the left (1400 px in 0.2 s).

3.0: the rails clap shut on it and reopen, stretching DESIGNER out of the line; its letters then fly out sideways.

3.5: CLAUDE in blue pencil, letters dropping from above one every 0.05 s. At 4.0 the rails close and crush it into one line 1476 px long.

Bar 3, CURVES, 4-6 s, paper.

4.1: the line gets pen-tool handles (430 px long at 58 degrees, small squares at the ends, circles on the handle tips, the label EASE) and bends into an S.

4.5: the handles swing to the mirror angle; eight blue copies fan out 34 px apart, joined at both ends like a leaf.

5.0: handles retract; the ribbon becomes travelling sine waves (amplitude 92 px, 2.75 cycles, each line a little out of phase).

5.5: it gathers back into one flat line.

Bar 4, SHAPE MORPH, 6-8 s, paper.

6.1: the line curls into a circle of radius 235 (curvature grows, length stays). 6.5: triangle, turning 120 degrees as it changes. 7.0: square. 7.5: hexagon, point up, radius 270. Blue hatching builds inside, then cross-hatching.

Bar 5, TILING, 8-10 s, paper.

8.0: the hexagon shrinks to radius 96 and six more slide out around it. 8.5: twelve more, a honeycomb of

19. 9.0: dense hatching sweeps across until every cell is solid blue. 9.6 to 10.0: the centre cell's shape grows past the frame with a hard edge; inside it is the blueprint, with the honeycomb in white line.

Bar 6, 2D TO 3D, 10-12 s, blueprint.

10.0: three lines draw inside every hexagon, plus three dashed hidden ones: each is a cube seen corner-on. 

10.5: the eighteen outer cubes slide into the centre one, which grows to radius 270. 11.0: it turns a quarter and perspective switches on. 11.5: it faces front.

Bar 7, MECHANISM, 12-14 s, blueprint.

12.0: the cube flattens and its front square grows teeth: a 16-tooth gear, pitch radius 208. From 12.25 the train steps 45 degrees on every eighth note. 12.5: a 10-tooth gear grows out to the upper right, meshing. 13.0: a 12-tooth gear to the upper left. Each has a dashed pitch circle, a hub and a label (16T, 10T, 12T). 13.5: the small gears retract; the gear becomes a square again and the cube gets its depth back.
Bar 8, UNFOLD, 14-16 s, blueprint.

14.0: the cube unfolds on its hinges into a cross of six squares. 14.5: the squares slide and stretch into six panels: a header strip, a tall sidebar, a wide chart, two tiles, a timeline strip.

15.0: they fill in. Header: "CLAUDE — MOTION REEL", a BARS / RING switch, a LIGHT toggle. Chart: 30 bars, one per second of this film, heights 42 30 36 44 50 46 52 62 50 56 62 72 60 66 58 76 56 62 68 74 70 78 86 94 100 93 97 90 80 50. Timeline: the 15 bar names, a keyframe diamond on each.
15.5: counters roll up: 120 BPM, 60 BEATS, 1800 FRAMES, 0 CUTS.
Bar 9, DATA, 16-18 s, blueprint.

16.0: a graph line draws across the bar tops; a cyan playhead lands on the timeline at the real time. The current second's bar is solid cyan, earlier ones hatched, later ones outlined. A cursor arrives.
16.5: it clicks RING: the chart's baseline bends round into a circle of radius 110 with the ba

title: Rocket launch from an ocean platform at dawn
text:
Create a cinematic, highly detailed, interactive 3D rocket launch from an ocean platform at dawn. Deliver the complete project in one HTML file that opens directly in Chrome. Use Three.js + WebGL and procedural assets. Embed assets wherever practical; a reliable CDN may be used for the rendering library.

ART DIRECTION
Create a dramatic transition from a dark, blue-violet ocean before sunrise to warm sunlight above the atmosphere. Use convincing proportions, detailed materials, atmospheric depth, and carefully composed camera angles. The result should feel like a polished miniature spaceflight film.
ROCKET AND LAUNCH PLATFORM
Build a convincing multistage rocket with a shaped nose cone, panel seams, structural rings, interstage connections, engine nozzles, and a payload fairing that separates into two halves.

Create a detailed floating launch platform with a support tower, retracting strongback, service arms, railings, ladders, pipes, equipment, floodlights, and blinking warning beacons. Keep all structures physically connected and correctly positioned.
LAUNCH SEQUENCE
Create an approximately 46-second sequence:

Establishing camera move around the platform.

Service arms and strongback retract.
Engines ignite, illuminating the rocket, platform, and nearby water.
Smoke spreads across the deck as the rocket lifts off and accelerates.
The camera follows the climb from the atmosphere toward space.
The first stage separates and falls away.
The second-stage engine ignites.
The fairing halves separate, revealing a satellite.
The engine shuts down, the satellite deploys, and its solar panels unfold.
Finish with an orbital view of the satellite against Earth’s curved horizon and sunrise.
Compress the flight timeline for presentation while maintaining coherent motion. Avoid sudden position changes, intersecting components, or disconnected effects.
OCEAN, ATMOSPHERE, AND EFFECTS
Use animated shader-driven ocean waves with Fresnel reflections and warm engine-light reflections. Create layered exhaust with a bright core, softer outer flame, and drifting smoke particles.
Smoke should expand, fade, and respond to wind. Exhaust must remain attached to the correct engine through staging. Transition smoothly from atmospheric haze to a dark star field and Earth’s illuminated limb.

CAMERA AND INTERACTION
Use smooth cinematic camera transitions: wide establishing view, low-angle ignition shot, ascent tracking, stage separation, and satellite close-up. Keep the main subject visible in both portrait and landscape layouts.

Include play/pause, replay, and a scrubber with event markers. Seeking must reconstruct the correct rocket configuration, particle state, camera position, and lighting. Replaying must reset the entire sequence cleanly.
Keep the interface minimal and unobtrusive. Allow it to be hidden for recording.

TECHNICAL QUALITY
Use frame-rate-independent animation and efficient particle systems. Reuse geometry and materials where appropriate, handle resizing correctly, and balance visual detail with smooth performance.

THE WATERMELON
Create a thick, rounded triangular watermelon wedge with:
Translucent ruby-red jelly flesh.
A pale, slightly translucent layer between the flesh and rind.
A glossy green outer rind with irregular dark-green stripes.

Individually modeled dark seeds embedded in both exposed sides.
Softly rounded corners and an appealing, substantial thickness.
Make it look like an expensive gummy candy photographed in a studio. It should feel juicy, soft, and almost edible. Keep the colors rich without overexposing the highlights.
SOFT-BODY PHYSICS
Use a volumetric soft-body simulation, such as a tetrahedral mesh with XPBD elastic and volume-preservation constraints.
The user must be able to:
Grab the tip, a corner, the flesh, or the rind.
Stretch, bend, lift, and gently twist the slice.

Release it and watch it wobble before gradually settling.
The slice must visibly deform locally, not simply move or scale as one rigid object. Make the rind slightly firmer than the flesh while keeping the whole slice flexible.
Preserve volume reasonably during stretching. Prevent inverted elements, explosive motion, and permanent collapse. Use a fixed simulation timestep and bounded substeps for stability.
After release, the motion should decay naturally - no instant snapping back and no endless oscillation.
Keep seeds attached to the deforming flesh. They must move and rotate with the surface rather than float independently or remain fixed in space.
Include ground contact, gentle friction, and soft bouncing. Avoid visible floor penetration.
RENDERING
Use native WebGPU with WGSL shaders.
Include:
Thickness-dependent light absorption.
Refraction through the jelly.

Fresnel reflections and glossy highlights.
Soft transmitted light through thin edges.
Subtle internal details and a few tiny air bubbles.

Soft contact shadows beneath the slice.
A light, neutral studio background.
The flesh, pale rind, and green skin should have distinct material responses. Avoid making everything look like clear glass or opaque plastic.
Keep the slice large and easy to inspect, with a three-quarter camera angle that reveals the flesh, seeds, and thickness.
INTERFACE
Use a minimal editorial layout with generous whitespace, thin borders, restrained controls, and no decorative UI gradients.
Top left:
“MATERIAL STUDIES / NO. 009”
A large italic serif heading split across two lines: “Melon” and “Jelly.”
Small caption:
“A slice of summer.”
“A little wobble.”
“Too soft to share.”
Top right:
A small status indicator showing “WEBGPU · LIVE” when the renderer is running.

Right-side panel:
“THE SPECIMEN”
Three coordinated watermelon-inspired color presets.
Firmness slider with its current value.
Internal damping slider with its current value.
“Give it a nudge” and “Reset” buttons.
“¼ speed” and “Show mesh” checkboxes.

Pause / Resume button.
Bottom left:
A short hint explaining that the slice can be grabbed and stretched.
Live mass, relative volume, and kinetic-energy readouts derived from the simulation. Clearly describe illustrative units or approximate values where appropriate.
Bottom right:

A collapsible “Inside the experiment” section briefly explaining the physics and rendering.
BEHAVIOR AND PERFORMANCE
Support both mouse and touch input. Use pointer capture so dragging remains reliable when the pointer leaves the object.
Make the layout work on desktop and mobile without controls covering the slice.
Reuse buffers and avoid rebuilding geometry or compiling shaders during dragging. Keep interaction smooth and responsive.
Respect reduced-motion preferences. If WebGPU is unavailable, display a clear explanation instead of silently substituting a fake renderer.
VALIDATION
Test dragging from several locations, strong stretches, repeated releases, ground collisions, all sliders, presets, pause, reset, and slow motion.
Check that the model returns to a stable resting shape, seeds stay attached, the mesh remains intact, and there are no rendering errors.
Prioritize the quality of the jelly response and lighting. The result should be something people want to keep grabbing and playing with.

text:

Hand: hold=Press, inward drag=Squeeze, outward drag=Grab, fast release=Throw. Use weighted grabs, smoothed 3D target, pointer velocity and momentum. Cake remains free; cake input overrides orbit.
Knife: procedural 3D knife. Draw a cut line; animate contact→compression→penetration→breakthrough→lift. Deform before splitting; keep seam thin.
Repeated cutting is mandatory: use a dynamic pieces list; every piece stays cuttable. Convert strokes to vertical cut planes, split crossed pieces, create new soft-body/render meshes, transfer deformation/velocity, preserve toppings, keep halves aligned, update Pieces. Support 14+ pieces and multi-piece cuts. No fixed whole/left/right states.
Drop releases all pieces. Reset restores one intact cake and Pieces=1. Use fixed timestep/substeps, DPR≤2, clamp instability, avoid NaNs/GPU errors. Expose window.__cake.
Run locally, test interactions and repeated cutting, and iterate until polished.

title: Fictional Fashion Commercial Direction with Claude Opus 5.5 and MiniMax H3
text:
subject_definitions:
<Subject 1> is the model in <Picture 1>, including their face, skin tone, hairstyle, hair color, body proportions, and outfit exactly as shown.
<Subject 2> is the wearable product in <Picture 2>, including its exact silhouette, proportions, colors, materials, surface finish, and any printed label or logo design exactly as they appear in the image.

summary:
[reference generation] The target video is a 15-second cinematic fashion commercial in which <Subject 1> wears <Subject 2>. It is built as eight 1.5-second scenes followed by a 3-second hero finale. Each scene changes location, lighting, and composition on the beat, and in each scene one short word exists physically inside the environment. The finale is a full-frame hero shot in front of giant illuminated letters spelling "QUIVRE", with the tagline "Carry your own light." and the call to action "SHOP NOW".

retention_analysis:
<Subject 1> (appears in [Shot 2], [Shot 4], [Shot 5], [Shot 6], [Shot 7], [Shot 8], [Shot 9]): fully_preserved - the face, skin tone, hairstyle, hair color, body proportions, and outfit from <Picture 1> stay identical throughout; if <Subject 2> is a clothing item, footwear, or accessory, it replaces only the matching item of that outfit.
<Subject 2> (appears in [Shot 1] to [Shot 9]): fully_preserved - the shape, proportions, colors, materials, surface finish, and logo from <Picture 2> stay identical in every shot.

detailed_description:
The target video is a photoreal cinematic fashion commercial shot at blue hour and night, with low-key lighting, strong backlight and rim light, drifting atmospheric haze, wet reflective surfaces, deep contrast, and a color scheme of cool steel-blue shadows against the warm glow of <Subject 2>'s own dominant color. <Subject 1> is the only person, and <Subject 2> is the only featured product, worn naturally and always clearly visible and in focus. Every word of text exists physically inside the scene and is spelled exactly as written; it never covers the face or the product, and no other text appears.
[Shot 1] Total darkness filled with slow-moving haze. A narrow horizontal blade of white light sweeps across the frame and projects the word "QUIVRE" in thin, widely spaced capital letters onto a dark concrete wall. As the blade passes, it catches <Subject 2> worn by <Subject 1> in the foreground in a tight close-up, rim-lighting its edges and igniting its warm color. The camera pushes in slowly. A deep bass hit lands with the light sweep.
[Shot 2] At 00:01.500, the shot cuts to a long concrete tunnel at blue hour with a blinding white backlight at its far end and haze in the air. <Subject 1>, wearing <Subject 2>, walks out of the backlight from silhouette toward the camera, passing between enormous freestanding concrete letters spelling "NEW" that stand on both sides of the path. The camera tracks backward at a low angle. Heavy footsteps echo.
[Shot 3] At 00:03.000, the shot cuts to an extreme macro of <Subject 2> on the body of <Subject 1> in a dark room. A hard spotlight passes through a metal stencil and casts the word "DETAIL" as sharp letter-shaped light onto the dark wall behind, while the camera glides across the product's material texture and edges in raking light.
[Shot 4] At 00:04.500, the shot cuts to a windswept rooftop at dusk under a deep blue sky. Behind <Subject 1>, a huge white fabric banner printed with the black word "FREE" billows and snaps violently in the wind. Their hair whips across their face as they turn back toward the camera, <Subject 2> clearly visible. The camera circles at a low angle. Wind roars and fabric cracks.
[Shot 5] At 00:06.000, the shot cuts to a rain-soaked city crosswalk at night. Large white road-painted letters reading "EVERY DAY" lie across the wet asphalt, glistening with reflected streetlights and blurred traffic lights. <Subject 1> strides across the letters while the camera tracks alongside at the height of <Subject 2>, the painted words sliding through the foreground. Water splashes softly under each step.
[Shot 6] At 00:07.500, the shot cuts to a tall glass wall in a dark modern building lit by cold blue light from outside. The word "LIGHT" is etched large into the glass in the foreground. Behind the glass, <Subject 1> walks from left to right with <Subject 2> visible through the clear parts of the glass, their figure passing behind the etched letters. The camera slides sideways, creating strong parallax between the letters and the model.
[Shot 7] At 00:09.000, the shot cuts to a dark studio with haze. Enormous three-dimensional letters spelling "BOLD" stand behind <Subject 1>, sculpted from the same material and color as <Subject 2> and lit by one hard top light that throws deep shadows. <Subject 1> holds a still, confident full-body pose in front of them, wearing <Subject 2> on the body exactly as in the other shots; <Subject 2> is large, sharply lit, and never hidden or left out. The camera snap-zooms in on the beat. A punchy whoosh-and-hit accent lands.
[Shot 8] At 00:10.500, the shot cuts to a close-up of <Subject 1>'s face together with <Subject 2> beside a night window. Outside, a warm illuminated sign spelling "YOURS" is reflected in the window glass next to their face, blurred by raindrops. <Subject 1> looks directly into the camera with a calm, confident expression. The camera pushes in very slowly. Rain taps softly on the glass.
[Shot 9] At 00:12.000, the shot cuts to a newly staged, full-frame wide shot of a vast dark studio that fills the entire frame edge to edge, with no black bars, borders, or framed picture. Giant freestanding illuminated letters spelling "QUIVRE" glow warm white across the back of the set, reflected on the glossy black floor. <Subject 1> stands slightly right of center, large in the frame from head to knees and filling about two-thirds of the frame height, in a composed hero pose while wearing <Subject 2>, which is sharply lit by a spotlight and clearly readable as the hero product. In the empty lower-left area of the frame, clean white text "Carry your own light." fades in, then "SHOP NOW" appears inside a thin rounded outline button beneath it, never over the model's body. The camera stays locked off with no zoom or push-in so the whole face always stays in frame, and the final half second holds completely still like a printed advertising key visual. A final bass hit rings out with a long shimmering tail.

overall_soundscape:
Cinematic, close foley throughout, with whooshes on every cut and a low room hum under the finale. No voices or narration.

non_diegetic_music:
A dark, stylish electronic track at about 80 BPM with a deep sub-bass, a hard kick and snap, metallic percussion, and tense pulsing synths. Every cut lands on every second beat. It builds from [Shot 4], peaks at [Shot 7], then drops to silence for a breath before a final huge bass hit at 00:12.000 and a long reverb tail.

I want to test your video creation capabilities. I want you to create a launch-style video (like when Anthropic launches a new feature) to use as an App Store preview video. Look up best practices and what converts best for these types of videos.

To create the video, use only JavaScript, Playwright, and FFmpeg. I added the hyperframes skill and you can use it if you deem it necessary. Be creative and fun, aligned with the communication we already use in the App.
