title: Meteor Time-Freeze Cinematic Sequence Prompt Orchestrated by Opus 5.5
text:
[Identity Lock | Woman]
Adult female, ~28, straight black hair, fair skin, dark brown eyes; knee-length bright red wool coat, black jeans, black ankle boots; red coat is the dominant color; continuous single actor, no face-swapping or outfit changes.

[Identity Lock | Man]
Adult male, ~30, short dark brown hair, light stubble, light olive skin; navy jacket, grey hoodie, dark jeans; holding two white paper coffee cups without logos; continuous single actor, no face-swapping or outfit changes.

[Space]
Fixed geography: ~15m wide two-lane urban street flanked by storefronts; warm-lit cafe on left with glass door facing street; glass bus stop on right facing cafe; street extends to horizon; meteor streaks from top right to horizon, exploding outside city; dust wall surges towards camera; he exits cafe on left, she waits at bus stop on right, meeting in street center without screen direction inversion; ~10 pedestrians.

[First Frame]
24mm low-angle wide shot looking down street; quiet night street, shop lights, streetlamps, dark sky; top-right sky glows bright orange-white.

[Timeline / SHOT 1]
0.0–4.0s | 24mm low wide upward tilt: 0.0–1.5s sky lights up brighter than day, cast shadows swing rapidly; 1.5–3.0s pedestrians gaze up as massive burning meteor streaks across top-right sky towards horizon; 3.0–4.0s meteor glare reflects on cafe door glass, creating first match cut.

[Timeline / SHOT 2]
4.0–9.0s | Match cut from glare, 35mm handheld outside cafe: 4.0–5.5s he pushes door open holding two coffees, looks up and halts; 5.5–7.0s he sees her across the street at the bus stop, eyes meet; 7.0–8.0s both sprint into street; 8.0–9.0s massive white explosion at horizon washes out screen, creating second match cut.

[Timeline / SHOT 3]
9.0–15.0s | Match cut from whiteout, 35mm elevated street view: 9.0–11.0s whiteout fades to mushroom cloud and orange fireball; 11.0–13.5s shockwave blasts storefront windows successively towards camera, alarms blare, dust wall rolls forward; both sprint towards street center; 13.5–15.0s nearest window shatters toward lens, creating third match cut.

[Timeline / SHOT 4]
15.0–19.0s | Match cut from flying glass, 50mm eye-level profile, both in street center: 15.0–17.0s reaching out, he drops both coffees, liquid spills, glass whirls, dust wall 20m away, wind pulls hair; 17.0s time abruptly freezes completely; 17.0–19.0s absolute standstill except she slowly blinks, creating fourth match cut.

[Timeline / SHOT 5]
19.0–25.0s | Match cut from blink, 35mm handheld over her right shoulder: 19.0–20.5s realizing she can move, she looks around; 20.5–23.5s steps forward through suspended shards, gently deflects a floating glass shard which stays in place; passes frozen coffee spill, frozen pigeon, frozen pedestrians, frozen fiery dust wall; 23.5–25.0s approaches him and reaches out, creating fifth match cut.

[Timeline / SHOT 6]
25.0–30.0s | Match cut from reaching hand, 50mm close profile: 25.0–26.5s fingertips touch his frozen cheek; 26.5–28.0s he blinks, inhales, looks at her and unfreezes, clasping her hand; 28.0–30.0s adjacent suspended glass shard vibrates and drops; both watch it fall; scene cuts mid-fall.

[Physics]
Meteor illumination realistically shifts street shadows; shockwave shatters glass sequentially outward; dust wall is volumetric fire/dust; time freeze is total for all background elements with zero motion blur or drift; deflected shard stays at new position; gravity resumes on moving subjects; only final shard vibrates and drops.

[Cinematography]
6 sequential camera setups; 5 match cuts matched to ending elements (reflection, flash, shard, blink, hand); camera static during freeze except Shot 5 tracking; no slow motion, no hero low-angles.

[Lighting/Color]
Opens cold blue with warm shop light; switches to harsh orange-white under meteor; orange-red explosion lighting; frozen world back-lit by fire inside dust wall; red coat remains focal point.

[Audio]
Shot 1 quiet traffic to escalating roar; Shot 2 doorbell, footsteps, distant impact; Shot 3 blast roar, shattering windows, alarms; Shot 4 wind/glass noise abruptly cuts to dead silence at 17s; Shot 5 quiet footsteps on glass and soft breath; Shot 6 sharp inhale and gentle glass hum.

[Locks]
Strictly 6 shots, 5 match cuts; zero spoken dialogue; continuous outfits and character identities without fusion; exact anatomical consistency; live-action film realism; video cuts while the shard falls.

title: Double Pendulum Chaos Simulation with 1e-9 Radian Separation
text: Simulate three double pendulums in Python: 1 kg bobs, 1 m massless rods, g = 9.81 m/s². All start at rest with both arms at 120° from vertical; copy 2 has its upper arm 1e-9 rad further out, copy 3 has 2e-9 rad. Integrate 40 s accurately and save the full state at 30 fps.

title: First-Person 3D Procedural Arms and Dynamic Grip Rigging in Three.js
text:
TASK: Build production-grade first-person arms ("Hands 2.0") for a Three.js browser game, then fix them until every pose actually holds the object it should hold. Do the whole thing yourself with scripts, from generating the model to the in-game checks. I already did this once. Below is what works and the traps I fell into, so you don't repeat them.

━━━ PART 1 — THE MODEL (Blender + MPFB2, fully scripted) ━━━

1. Don't patch AI-generated "statue" arms (Meshy etc.). Chaotic topology with no edge loops at the joints and fingers baked into a pose will crease at every bend. Without clavicle and twist bones the wrist twists like a candy wrapper. Gluing separate generated parts together only adds seams to the same bad mesh. Start over with a real humanoid generator.

2. Use Blender (headless: `blender --background --python tools/hands/*.py`) + MPFB2 (MakeHuman, CC0) and its official asset packs. Put every step in a script so it can be rebuilt:
   - build_body.py: macro params (male, ~30 y/o, wiry and lean: muscle ~0.66, weight ~0.3) plus local arm targets.
   - build_arms.py: game skeleton with clavicle → shoulder → upperarm01/02 → lowerarm01/02 (twist bones!) → wrist → metacarpals → 3 phalanges per finger. Keep skin only from the elbow down and apply subdiv 1. Make the sleeve a separate mesh on the same bones, with real geometry for the rolled cuff. Accessories (watch, bracelet) are parented to forearm/wrist bones; watch hands are bones too.
   - build_tex.py: UVs, then bake veins, tendons and knuckles into geometry and normals. Author every detail in bone-local 3D space so it survives re-UVs, then bake in Cycles.
   - https://t.co/3ocKmFbTLm → pack script → hands_v2.glb. Budget ~25–40k tris for both arms incl. sleeves (they're huge on screen), 1–2 skin materials + sleeve + accessories. Textures 2048² on High, 1024² on Low, plus a tiling micro-normal for pores.
   - Generate a full body with pants, boots and the same shirt, and save it as a .blend for a future "player body" stage. Don't put it in the game yet.

3. Look: tanned back of hand and forearm, paler palm and inner side. Scars, calluses, short nails with natural cuticles. Flannel sleeves rolled just below the elbow, with a visible inside-out lining on the roll. Tactical watch on the left wrist, cord bracelet on the right.

4. Check skin weights on stress poses before you export: fist, pinch, spread fingers, 90° supination. Fix weights in a script, not by hand.

5. HARD STOP #1: render review shots in Blender (neutral light and warm daylight): front, back, palms, fist, pinch, cylinder grip, spread fingers, sleeve close-up, two plaid colour variants. Wait for my verbal OK. Iterate. Don't integrate anything into the game until I say yes.

6. glTF only gives you standard material slots, so use them as carriers. Example: MR = (R AO, G roughness, B subsurface thickness), emissive = masks (R hair, G dirt accumulation order), clearcoatNormal = pore tile. Document the mapping and read it back in the runtime.

━━━ PART 2 — SHADERS (MeshStandard/Physical + onBeforeCompile) ━━━

- Skin: wrap lighting, back-lit translucency in thin areas (fingers, webbing, knuckles go red against the sun), pore detail normal, micro-sheen, tan gradient by mask.
- Hair: 4 fur shells in ONE instanced draw, only on hairy triangles, visible on the silhouette against the sun. Disabled on Low.
- Dynamic state:
  · wet = max(world wetness, rain when not under a roof), with two layers of droplets. The sleeve goes darker when wet.
  · dirt builds up from game events (gather, pickup, log, fish_land, climb_out…), fingers and palms first through the mask, and washes off in water or rain.
- Arm lighting mirrors the world: shade under roofs, lamp light, lightning.
- Precompile every arm shader behind the loading screen. https://t.co/nXMh9v1zBi.programs.length must not grow during gameplay.
- Budget: the arm overlay may cost at most ~0.3 ms more GPU than before on High. Measure with a timer query before and after, not by feel.

━━━ PART 3 — THE ARM SYSTEM (data, not code) ━━━

Goal: a new item or action (axe, bow, paddle, steering wheel) should be a data entry plus a clip, never new logic.

1. Rig wrapper: bone map, wrist twist spread over the twist bones (e.g. 0.3 / 0.8 on lowerarm01/02). No candy-wrapper wrists.
2. Two-bone IK (shoulder–elbow–wrist) with pole vectors (elbows down and out) and joint limits.
3. grips.js: for each item, per hand: `at / axis / back / r / diag / gap / slide / fingers / thumb` in item space. One hand owns the item, the other IKs to its socket.
4. Fingers are always a joint table `[[mcp, pip, dip, spread, twist] × 5]` (absolute bend) and blend between poses. Autogrip closes the fingers until they touch the handle.
5. Animation layers, in this order: base pose → clip keyframes → IK → procedural (breath, bob, mouse-turn inertia, sway, recoil, fatigue tremor) → additive reactions. Smooth transitions between states.
6. Clips: JSON keyframes in code, plus importing .glb animations (with empty hand_R/hand_L) for future Blender-made actions. Clip events (strike frame, bow release) go onto the effects bus.
7. In-game pose editor (Shift+H, game keeps running, cursor free): sliders for item offset and rotation, sockets, every finger joint, elbow pole, shoulders, layer speeds. Show changes live. "Copy" puts JSON on the clipboard to paste into grips.js. I need to be able to tune a grip without Blender.
8. Keep the old public API as a facade (hands.anim, reach, lampInHand…) so fishing, boat, lamp, weapons, sleep and the seaplane don't need deep rewrites.
9. Port EVERY existing action: rifle (stance, ADS, fire, reload with mag, dry fire), knife (2 strikes), stone throw, fishing rod (cast, fight, reel, fish in hand), carried log, lamp, reach and pickup, plant gathering, inspect, crate, swimming (breaststroke and crawl), boat tiller, hands down while sleeping, hidden arms in vehicles. Each one must be at least as good as before. Delete the old arm code only after everything is ported (keep a backup).
10. HARD STOP #2: in-game screenshots for my approval (idle, rifle, rod, log, lamp at night, wet after swimming, dirty after firewood, under a roof and in full sun).

━━━ PART 4 — THE FIX PASS (bake this in from day one) ━━━

The first version shipped with these bugs. Every one of them came from old poses written for "stump" arms with no shoulder.

ROOT CAUSE: a real arm has a fixed length (shoulder→wrist ≈ 0.48 m in view space). Old poses put wrists at targets the arm can't reach. The solver then "cheated": it pushed the clavicle out (up to 0.32 m) and clamped the wrist rotation. The hand ended up somewhere else, while finger curls were cached for the ideal hand position, so the fingers squeezed thin air.
  - Rifle, left hand: handguard 0.516 m away with a 0.479 m arm → shoulder pushed out ~0.3 m and the fist still sat 3.8 cm below the handguard.
  - Rifle, right hand: wrist rotation clamped by ~21°, palm not seated on the grip.

FIXES, as SYSTEM features:
1. Shoulder stance as data: per item/pose, `stance: { L:[x,y,z], R:[x,y,z] }` with smooth blending, and the elbow pole moves with the shoulder. Rifle: left shoulder forward and in, right shoulder slightly back (a real shooter's torso rotation). The left elbow stays slightly bent and the clavicle doesn't stretch.
2. Elbow auto-swivel: give each forearm a pronation range (e.g. R −100°…+95°, 0 = thumb up). If the requested pole would over-twist the forearm or bend the wrist past its limit, rotate the elbow around the shoulder–wrist line to the nearest valid angle. The old poses were silently over-twisted (+101° on the rifle, +80° on the knife).
3. Grip by the REAL handle shape. A cylinder radius is wrong: the knife handle was a 2.6 × 4.2 cm oval, not Ø2.5 cm, so the knuckles sank 2–6 mm into it.
   - Handle = elliptical cylinder with end caps (`sec` [along back, across], `span`, `inset`).
   - measureSection(item, socket): take the cross-section automatically by slicing the item mesh around `at` along `axis`.
   - CPU-skin the hand (SkinnedMesh.getVertexPosition, palm and phalanx vertices with weights) and test real skin vertices, not phalanx tips.
   - gripFit, cached and computed at startup: first push the palm out until it leaves the handle. Then close each finger with all joints together until first contact, and after that only the joints past the touching phalanx. If the start pose already intersects, open it up.
   - Fingertip targets: `fingers: {1: {to:[x,y,z]}}` puts the index pad on the trigger.
4. Validator: hands.check(pose) and hands.checkAll(). Run every scenario × both hands + the live rod pose, print a console table, and show it live in the Shift+H editor with a "Check all poses" button. RED if wrist miss > 0.5 cm, rotation clamp > 3°, shoulder push > 0.5 cm, twist over the limit > 3°, or any skin vertex deeper than 1.5 mm inside the handle. Don't call the work done until it's all green (mine ended at 122/122).

DATA FIXES that came from my screenshots:
- Rifle: left hand on the WOODEN handguard, not the metal in front of it. Handguard runs diagonally across the palm, thumb along the left side, forearm coming in from the lower-left corner. Right hand fully on the pistol grip using the grip's real rake (axis (0, 0.95, −0.32), not a guessed 40°), index on the trigger. On reload the hand leads and the mag rides in the hand, and the shoulder dips to follow it. Check sprint, recoil, dry fire, and steering a boat while holding the rifle.
- Log: nobody carries a 44 × 7 cm log with two arms like a crate. One hand, an ordinary hammer grip like a bottle: knuckles up, thumb on top, held about a third from the back end, log pointing forward and up from the thumb side, riding in the fist. The throw is a one-handed wind-up and lunge. The left hand stays free, so the lamp stays in it.
- Swimming: fingers together and slightly cupped (no fan), hands in the bottom third of the frame. Crawl recovery comes in from the side, palm facing out. The sleeve never covers the middle of the screen and the palm never faces the camera.
- Fix every pose the validator flags: stone wind-up and throw, aim, lamp, lamp lowered, climbing, reach.

━━━ RULES ━━━
- Backup before each stage. Measure, don't guess: write every claim down as a number (cm, °, ms, tris, programs).
- No performance regression: grip fit is cached per socket, and the validator only runs in the editor or dev builds.
- Write down what's still unfinished honestly in the report (e.g. "right hand mostly below the frame on the rifle", "pinky sometimes curls without contact").
- DONE = I approved the renders and the screenshots, bends are clean on every grip, fingers wrap handles with zero penetrations, wet and dirt work, every old action works on the new system, a new item is one grips.js entry + one clip, and FPS is unchanged.

title: Interactive 3D Dino Jelly Diorama in Three.js
text:

A translucent, wobbly jelly cube floats in the middle of the page like a collectible diorama. Inside the top layer lives a tiny prehistoric island: a lush jungle of palms and giant ferns, a smoking volcano, a baby T-Rex, a long-neck brontosaurus, a few eggs in a nest and a fossil skull half buried in the sand. - The T-Rex blinks and roars every few seconds (head tilt + jelly ripple); the brontosaurus slowly turns its neck; palms sway.
- Camera: slow orbit, OrbitControls

title: Please use Three.js to write a single-file HTML (index.html) to…
text:
Please use Three.js to write a single-file HTML (index.html) to create a "hiking documentary style" 3D scene for screen recording narration videos.

[Basic Requirements]
- Import Three.js via CDN (cdnjs or jsdelivr), no build tools required, runnable directly by double-clicking in a browser.
- Strict 16:9 aspect ratio, designed internally at 1920x1080, centered with aspect ratio maintained and black bars filled when resizing.
- All adjustable parameters (terrain seed, route points, camera speed, etc.) centralized in a CONFIG object at top of file.

[Terrain]
- Use multi-layer noise (Simplex/Perlin, self-implemented) to generate a north-south mountain gorge: high mountains on both sides, valley bottom in the middle with a winding riverbed.
- Color by elevation and slope: deep brown/gray ridges, earthy yellow slopes, light yellow valley, blue-gray riverbed, light snow on peaks.
- Add fog and directional light to create a cold, dry plateau atmosphere.

[Route & Character]
- Define hiking route using a list of (x, z) waypoints in CONFIG, smooth with CatmullRomCurve3 matching terrain height.
- Render route as thick red line (subtle glow), passed section bright red, upcoming section semi-transparent.
- Red low-poly figure (capsule + sphere head + red coat) walking along route at constant speed, adjustable speed, supports pause.
- Support event markers on route (e.g., Assembly point, Last seen), displayed as vertical signs with text or pulsing rings.

[Camera]
- Four modes switchable via keys 1-4 with smooth transitions:
  1. High overhead view (flying forward along route, slightly tilted)
  2. Follow (behind and above character)
  3. Orbit (slow orbit around character)
  4. Free look (drag to rotate, scroll zoom, WASD move)
- Camera speed, height, pitch angle adjustable in CONFIG.

[UI Overlay (HTML/CSS)]
- Columns of member cards on both sides: square avatar (solid color + initial placeholder, customizable via URL), name, role caption.
- Member status: Normal / Deceased (gray card with red border) / Missing (semi-transparent with question mark).
- Centered bottom subtitle bar, white text with black stroke, supports [[keyword]] yellow highlight.
- Top right shows "Episode X" title and progress bar (optional).

[Timeline Driven]
- Describe storyline in CONFIG with a TIMELINE array, each entry containing time (seconds) and action:
  { time: 0,  action: "camera", mode: 1 }
  { time: 3,  action: "subtitle", text: "Then why did you dare to [[join]]?", duration: 4 }
  { time: 8,  action: "walk", from: 0, to: 0.4 }
  { time: 15, action: "status", member: "Hu Yanglin", state: "missing" }
  { time: 20, action: "marker", at: 0.6, text: "Last seen" }
- Playback logic: Space to play/pause, R to reset, auto-trigger events at timestamps.
- Small debug panel top-left, press H to hide for clean recording.

[Sample Content]
- Preset 8 fictional members (Tie Gao - organizer, Qian Niao, Hu Yanglin, Mimi, Members 5-8), ~90s demo timeline covering overhead view, walking, event markers, status changes, ending subtitles.

[Code Requirements]
- Clearly partitioned code with Chinese comments (terrain, route, character, camera, UI, timeline).
- Stable 30fps+ on standard laptops, terrain resolution ~256x256 vertices.
- Explain how to modify route, avatars, and add timeline events after completion.

Physics: XPBD soft body on a hex lattice (shape-matched cells + tetrahedral volume preservation, live volume readout), skinned to the mesh, sitting under gravity on Coulomb friction. It breathes with its flanks, twitches its snout when it sniffs, and slowly rights itself toward the way it last walked. Curling into a ball is a second rest shape found once at load (the body led nose-to-tail and squeezed into a sphere so the stuffing can really take that shape); curling blends every cell's rest shape and every tet's rest volume toward it. Nothing holds the ball upright, so a push makes it roll; when it stops it unrolls and stands up again.

Spines: hundreds of soft felted cones rooted on the skin, rebuilt every frame from the skin's stretch and turn; they lie back toward the tail, stand up when it bristles or curls, lag behind every jolt on a damped spring, part around the finger and fold on the table instead of going through it. Cream root, dark band, pale tip, a short fuzz over each. The face, belly and paws wear minky shell fur that lies back from the nose and takes the comb.

Behaviours: Trundle (walks on its paws in diagonal pairs), Curl up, Roll, Bristle, Smooth fur, Reset. Hand: pick it up — hold it a moment and it curls into a prickly ball in your hand; put it down, squash it, throw it; bend a paw. Finger: it trundles over and sniffs your finger; run the finger through the spines and they part; poke its back and it huffs and rolls up. Comb: brush the minky. Sliders: Stuffing, Pile, Spines. title: Interactive 3D Squishy Toast Memory Foam Simulation
text:
Build "Squishy Toast" - a single self-contained HTML file (three.js from a CDN is the only dependency): an interactive 3D slice of slow-rise memory foam bread you can press, poke, stretch and squash.

The toast
- A real bread silhouette: square body, rounded "muffin top" crown, soft beveled edges

title: Interactive 3D Snow Globe Comparison
text:
Build "Snow Globe": a premium interactive 3D snow globe holding a tiny winter village, where every shake leaves a lasting, softly accumulating snowfall.
The emotional goal is the hush after shaking a real snow globe: "I want to shake it again and watch it settle."
ART DIRECTION
A heavy glass sphere rests on a turned walnut base on a warm linen tabletop. Inside: three cottages with steep roofs, a small chapel, a cluster of pines, a frozen pond and a lamppost. Use a palette of cream, frosted blue, pine green, brick red and warm window amber.
The glass should feel real: subtle refraction at the edges, a soft window-shaped highlight, a faint reflection of the room. Snow flakes are small, slightly irregular discs, not uniform dots. Accumulated snow is soft, rounded and matte.
CORE INTERACTION
Drag the globe to tilt and shake it.
Fast motion lifts settled snow into a swirling cloud.
Release to let the snow drift and settle.
Repeated shakes redistribute snow; gentle ones lift only the top layer.
The globe must follow the pointer closely, with a slight weighty lag. On phones, optional device-motion shaking after explicit permission.
THE SETTLING
Snow inherits the swirl of the liquid: it keeps circling, slows, and falls in lazy spirals. It accumulates as visible layers on roofs, branches, the lamppost cap and the pond. Thick snow slides off steep roofs in small clumps. The village lights glow brighter as the snow quiets.
Avoid snow passing through objects, sudden popping into place, or flat uniform coverage.
SOUND AND ATMOSPHERE
Optional sound: a soft liquid slosh linked to shake velocity, a faint glassy shimmer as snow falls, and a very distant chapel bell when everything has settled. Audio starts only after explicit activation. The scene must feel complete in silence.
TECHNICAL APPROACH
Use Three.js. Simulate the liquid as a simple damped swirl field driven by globe velocity. Store accumulation in a heightfield or per-surface snow map so it persists and builds. Keep the particle count modest and stable; reuse particles instead of creating new ones.
Keep the camera stationary while shaking; allow a restrained orbit when idle.
PRESENTATION
Show "Snow Globe", the hint "Shake gently. Watch it settle.", and discreet reset and sound controls.
Start with a light snowfall already drifting down so the scene is alive on arrival. No introduction modal.
DELIVERY AND PRIORITIES
Deliver a complete runnable browser experience with procedural geometry and textures and mouse/touch support. First perfect the shake-and-settle feel, then accumulation, then glass rendering and small details. Verify repeated shakes, full settling, reset, and stable performance on mobile. Include setup instructions.

title: Night Tokyo: Rainy Vending Machine 3D Diorama
text:
Build an interactive 3D web demo: **"Night Tokyo — Vending Machine"**.

A single Japanese vending machine standing alone on a rainy Tokyo street at night, presented as a small floating diorama. It is part of a series of minimal "Night Tokyo" miniatures, so the look matters more than the feature count: one object, rich materials, light and motion you want to keep watching.

## Deliverable
- One self-contained `index.html` in the current folder. Open it and it works: no build step, no server-only features.
- Three.js only, loaded from a CDN via an import map with an exact pinned version. Official Three.js addons (postprocessing, controls, etc.) are fine. No other libraries.
- No external assets: no image textures, models, fonts or audio files. Everything is procedural (geometry, canvas textures, shaders, Web Audio).

## The scene
- A cut-out slab of street (about 3×3 m) floating in darkness: wet asphalt with puddles and a strip of curb/sidewalk. The cut edges show a cross-section (asphalt layers, maybe a drain). Beyond the slab: darkness and falling rain.
- The vending machine is the main light source: a glowing front with two or three rows of drinks behind glass, a round selection button under each drink, a small price display, a coin/IC-card panel, and the pickup flap at the bottom. Fictional drink brands only; Japanese labels are welcome. At most one small prop next to it (e.g. a recycling bin for cans).
- Rain: streaks visible in the machine's light, ripples in the puddles.
- Wet ground: convincing reflections of the glowing machine and its colors in the asphalt and puddles. This is the key shot.
- Palette: deep blue-black night, warm white machine light, a few saturated accents from the drinks and buttons. Subtle bloom is fine; don't wash everything out.
- Small signs of life: e.g. the fluorescent tube occasionally flickers, the rain intensity varies slightly. Rare, small, believable.

## Interaction
- Hovering a selection button lights it up.
- Clicking buys the drink: the price display reacts, a mechanical sound plays, the can drops inside the machine, the pickup flap swings open and the can rolls out onto the wet pavement, settling with a believable bounce and roll. It stays there. Repeated purchases leave several cans on the ground (cap the count for performance and remove the oldest gracefully).
- Each drink has limited stock (e.g. 3). When it runs out, its 売切 (sold out) light turns on and the button no longer dispenses.
- Sound, synthesized with Web Audio: rain ambience, button click, can drop, can rolling on asphalt. Audio starts after the first user interaction. `M` toggles mute.
- Camera: a strong default 3/4 shot at roughly eye level, with the machine filling most of the frame height, and a slow, subtle idle drift. Drag to orbit within limited angles, scroll to zoom within limits. `C` resets to the default shot.
- UI: none, except a tiny unobtrusive hint that fades out after a few seconds.

## Quality bar
- Must look good at any aspect ratio, including narrow ones (around 8:9 and 9:16): it will be recorded side by side with another version.
- Smooth on a mid-range laptop: target 60 fps, cap devicePixelRatio at 2.
- No console errors.

## How to work
Work autonomously and don't ask clarifying questions; where something is unspecified, make the choice you think looks best. If your environment lets you open the page and look at it, do so and iterate on the visuals until you are happy with them. When finished, stop and briefly list what you built.

title: One-Tap Flying Mobile Game in HTML5 Canvas

between obstacles. Every gap you pass is +1 point. Hit anything and it's game over.

Requirements:

title: WebGPU XPBD Pineapple Jelly Interactive Soft-Body Simulation
text:
Build "Pineapple Jelly" — a single self-contained HTML file (inline JS/CSS, no libraries): a real-time WebGPU soft-body gummy pineapple ring with a real hole. The user can grab its outer or inner edge, stretch it, flip it over and let it wobble.

Object
- A thick canned-pineapple ring: outer radius 1.36, hole radius 0.5, thickness 0.5.
- Every edge rounded (bevel 0.12); 14 shallow scallops around the outer edge.
- Zones from rest-space coordinates, so they deform with the body. Both faces carry the same detail.
- A paler, denser core ring around the hole and a slightly deeper rim.
- Radial fibres: long thin streaks from core to rim, plus finer threads.
- The fibrous "eyes" band just inside the rim, where the flesh is most textured.
- Embedded juice cells (elongated pale sacs lying along the radius) and a few air bubbles that ride with the flesh.
- Tints: Golden, Amber, Rosé. Only the colour changes; scattering, gloss and fibres stay the same.

Physics (XPBD tetrahedral soft body)
- Mesh: 2D Delaunay of the scalloped annulus (outline samples plus a hex lattice; holes skipped), extruded into prisms → tets.
- Co-rotational per-tet shape matching (warm-started quaternion), so inverted tets recover; tet volume constraints for near-incompressibility; hard edge strain limits.
- Relative-velocity damping along edges; floor contact with Coulomb friction.
- Grab:
  - a soft patch attachment with bounded reach that never crushes the held patch into the floor;
  - the ray-pick knows when it passes through the empty hole;
  - scroll or a second finger twists the held patch.
- "Turn it over" tosses the ring with a spin about the screen's horizontal axis, so it flips and lands on its other face.
- Fixed 60 Hz step, small substeps (1 iteration each), gentle settling.
- The frame loop reuses every array (no per-frame allocation).

Rendering (WebGPU / WGSL)
- Passes: key-light shadow map; top-down height map for contact AO; scene (floor, juice cells, bubbles; MSAA); jelly back-face depth; jelly (refraction and absorption; MSAA) plus an optional mesh overlay; tone map.
- Procedural photo-studio cyclorama with softboxes. Soft PCSS key shadow tinted by the jelly.
- Jelly:
  - refraction of the scene by view-ray thickness;
  - per-tap Beer–Lambert absorption, denser and milkier in the core and fibres;
  - back-lit glow at thin edges, Fresnel studio reflections and GGX highlights.
- Post: exposure, Khronos PBR Neutral tone mapping, sRGB, dither.

UI (editorial "Material Studies / No. 012", English)
- Italic serif title "Pineapple / Jelly." and hint "Grab either edge. Pull. Let go."
- Panel "The Specimen": Tint swatches (tiny pineapple-ring icons); Firmness and Internal damping sliders; Give it a nudge, Turn it over, Reset, Pause; Show mesh and ¼ speed.
- Keys: Space to pause, N to nudge, T to turn it over, R to reset.
- Readouts: Mass (g, 1 unit ≈ 3 cm at 1.3 g/cm³), Volume (% of rest), Kinetic.
- Fallback screen when WebGPU is missing. Responsive stacked layout on mobile with no horizontal scroll.

title: Island Jelly: Interactive 3D Diorama with Surfing Rooster
text:
# Task: Build "Island Jelly", an interactive 3D diorama with a plush surfing rooster
Build a single self-contained `index.html` (no build step) using **three.js r165** via an importmap from jsDelivr (`three` + `three/addons/`). Use OrbitControls, RoomEnvironment and BufferGeometryUtils (`mergeGeometries`). It must run from any static server (e.g. `npx http-server`). It must look like a premium "material study": soft, tactile, toy-like, with cohesive materials. No cheap low-poly look.
---
## 1. Page & UI
- Background is warm paper `#E8E5DC`. Fonts are **Instrument Serif** italic for headings and **Inter** for UI, from Google Fonts.
- Top-left title block: tiny eyebrow "MATERIAL STUDIES", a big italic "Island Jelly.", a short rule, then a one-line subtitle: "A sandbar, three palms and a sea that wobbles back. Joe the rooster rides whatever you stir up."
- Top-right: a small pill showing the WebGL version and three.js revision.
- Right panel (frosted, 200px wide) contains:
  - **The sea:** buttons "Drop a pebble" and "Drop a coconut", plus counters for Afloat / Sunk / Ashore.
  - **Flavour:** three swatches that recolor the water: Lagoon `#35C8CC`, Raspberry `#F0457E`, Lime `#B4E03A`. Each has a matching deep and highlight color.
  - **Sliders:** Firmness (wave speed and stiffness), Wave damping, and Tide (raises or lowers the sea level and recomputes which cells are land).
  - **Buttons:** Reset, Pause, Reset view.
- Bottom-left "How to play" text. Hide the secondary text on mobile (<700px) and move the panel to the bottom-right.
## 2. Scene & rendering
- Renderer: antialias, alpha, pixel ratio capped at 2, PCFSoft shadows (2048 map), NeutralToneMapping.
- Environment: PMREM from RoomEnvironment at intensity ~0.55.
- Camera: perspective with a narrow 28° FOV, near-isometric view from (15.5, 14.5, 19).
- OrbitControls: damped, no pan, distance 12–50, max polar ~1.42. Left/right drag orbits, scroll zooms.
- Lights: a warm hemisphere light, plus a warm directional sun from the upper left that casts soft shadows.
- A large ShadowMaterial ground plane under the block.
## 3. The diorama block (10×10 units, everything in a `diorama` group that can tilt)
- **Sediment sides:** four planes whose UVs wrap around the block, textured with a procedural canvas showing strata. Layers from top to bottom: cream sand, a thin pink band, ochre, then dark brown. The band edges are wavy. Add soft grain and pale mineral inclusions in the lower bands. Close the block with a dark underside.
- **Terrain:** a 160×160 heightfield shared by seabed and island. The island is an irregular ellipse (perturbed with sin terms on its angle) that rises gently above sea level and falls off exponentially into the seabed. Add subtle ripple noise. Use sand vertex colors with slight variation.
- **Terrain shader** (onBeforeCompile):
  - Wet darkening near the waterline and a thin dark line exactly at the waterline.
  - Underwater tint from the water color to the deep color, by depth.
  - Animated procedural **caustics**, modulated by a texture built from the water heightfield's Laplacian, so caustics focus under wave crests and fade with depth.
- **Palms:** 3 curved trunks (CatmullRom tube) with ring-banded vertex colors and taper. Each crown has 8–9 droopy procedural fronds: a rib plus triangular leaflets in several greens. Add 3 coconuts in each crown. The crowns sway gently.
- **Pebbles:** a few squashed icosahedron pebbles in pastel greys and pinks around the island rim.
## 4. Water (the "jelly sea")
- A 100×100 heightfield wave simulation with a fixed step of 1/120 s:
  - Laplacian wave equation, plus a restoring spring and damping, all controlled by the sliders.
  - Land cells are masked out. Clamp the height range.
- **Tilt:** the block can be tilted by dragging its sides. Tilt is a damped spring. The equilibrium surface of the water tilts with it, so water sloshes from the walls. Local gravity is rotated into diorama space.
- **Surface mesh:** a 100×100 grid updated every frame with normals. Use MeshPhysicalMaterial with transmission 1, IOR 1.33, attenuation, and a tiling procedural ripple normal map that scrolls slowly.
- **Skirt:** a transmissive wall around the perimeter that follows the water edge height, plus thin bright highlight lines along the exposed water edges.
- **Interaction:**
  - Dragging on the water stirs waves, with strength based on drag speed.
  - Pebbles and coconuts can be grabbed and thrown.
  - Random drips make small ripples.
- **Objects:**
  - Pebbles sink. Coconuts float (they are plush spheres).
  - Both splash on entry, get buoyancy and drag, and are pushed by the wave gradient.
  - They collide with the terrain and walls, roll visually, and keep a state (air / afloat / sunk / ashore) that drives the counters.
## 5. Plush fur shader (used by the character and the coconuts)
Use shell fur: the base mesh plus N shells (10–12), each a copy of the mesh pushed out along its normal by `shell * len`. Implement it in `onBeforeCompile` on a MeshPhysicalMaterial (roughness ~0.92, sheen ~0.9, sheen color = base color lerped toward cream). Cache one material per (color, shell, len, rep, grav).
- **Vertex:** `transformed = position + normal*shell*len; transformed.y -= grav*shell²*len;`. This makes longer fur droop.
- **Fragment:**
  - Split the UVs into cells: `uv * vec2(rep, rep*0.5)`.
  - Each cell gets one **round strand** with a random height (0.4–1.0) and a jittered center.
  - Taper the radius toward the tip, and discard pixels outside the strand or above its height.
  - Shade darker at the roots and brighter at the tips: `mix(0.58, 1.07, pow(shell, 0.7))`. Add per-strand brightness variation.
- Only the base mesh casts shadows.
- Use a high strand density (rep ~200–250 on the main parts). Coarse strands look like needles up close.
## 6. The character: "Joe", a plush tribute to Chicken Joe from *Surf's Up*
**The goal is personality, not "a rooster".** He must be instantly recognisable as that laid-back, sleepy surfer chicken: lanky, slouched, half-asleep eyes, a lazy open-beak grin, a floppy red mohawk comb, a long scraggly neck, a pot belly and skinny legs. Render him as a high-quality plush toy (fur shader everywhere, felt for beak, legs and lids). Do not use flat feather cards.
Hierarchy: `surfer` (scale 1.35) → `boardTilt` → surfboard + `rooster` (scale ~0.56, rotated ~0.5 rad on the board) → `body` group (sways). All units below are rooster-local, with feet at y=0 and the character facing +z.
Palette:
| Name | Hex |
|---|---|
| Orange | `#EE9532` |
| Gold | `#F5B140` |
| Belly yellow | `#F8C653` |
| Rust | `#D9692A` |
| Comb red | `#DF2A2C` |
| Wing tips | `#26322A` |
| Beak | `#F7C433` |
| Legs | `#F4B43A` |
- **Surfboard:** a flattened sphere (0.34 × 0.045 × 0.82) in clearcoated cream, with a coral center stripe and a fin.
- **Legs:**
  - Thin felt tubes along a curve: foot (±0.16, 0.03) → bent knee (±0.155, 0.25, +0.08 forward) → hip (±0.1, 0.5).
  - Knobbly knee spheres.
  - Big feet: three long front toes splayed ±0.5 rad plus one back toe, as capsules.
  - A wide, relaxed stance.
- **Body (the slouch):**
  - Fuzzy rust "shorts" on the thighs.
  - An orange body ellipsoid, plus a yellow **pot belly pushed forward**, plus an upper chest/back leaning **backward**.
- **Neck:** a long fur tube along a curve from (0, 0.9, −0.05) to (0, 1.33, 0.13), curving forward. Use long drooping fur (len 0.06, grav 1.4). Wrap it in a **scraggly mane**:
  - About 6 rings of thin fuzzy cones pointing down and out, longer toward the bottom, plus a shaggy bib onto the chest.
  - Merge all the cones into two geometries (gold and orange) and plush each once, which saves draw calls.
  - Bury the cone roots inside the neck so no seams show.
- **Head:**
  - A fur sphere r=0.15 at (0, 1.38, 0.14).
  - A small tuft of fuzzy spikes at the back of the head.
- **Comb:**
  - A red base blade along the top of the head.
  - 5 fat rounded capsule lobes fanned from the forehead to the back (angles ~0.85 to −0.85 rad), with the middle lobes tallest and a slight alternating sideways flop.
  - Short velvet fur.
- **Eyes (the most important part):**
  - Big glossy white bulging eyes (r 0.075), close together and set high on the face. They must sit **outside** the head surface (eye center ≈ (±0.07, 0.085, 0.13), slightly turned outward). If they are buried, the lower white disappears.
  - Heavy **upper lids:** felt spherical caps covering ~56% of the sphere, tilted so the edge sits just at or below the eye's center. One lid is slightly droopier than the other. Add a thin darker rim torus on the lid edge.
  - A small **lower lid** cap pushed up from below, like cheeks from smiling.
  - Small dark pupils with a tiny highlight, peeking in the visible white band between the lids.
  - The resulting look is sleepy, stoned and content.
- **Beak (the grin):**
  - Upper beak: a long, wide, slightly flattened cone that curves gently downward at the tip (deform a ConeGeometry: widen x, flatten, bend by `hook * t^2.4`, and clamp t ≥ 0 to avoid NaN).
  - Lower beak: shorter, hinged open ~0.42 rad.
  - Dark red mouth interior and a pink tongue.
  - Orange-red cheek puffs at the corners of the mouth.
  - Two red wattles hanging under the beak.
- **Wings, held like loose arms:**
  - Shoulder pivots with rotation order ZYX.
  - A flattened orange fur forearm, a rust mid-section, and 5 dark fuzzy "finger" feathers fanned at the tip.
- **Tail:** a short, dark, scruffy spiky tuft angled up and back, on an orange fluffy base.
## 7. Animation & personality
- Ease everything. Nothing snaps and **nothing flaps**.
  - Smoothed wave energy: `enS += (en − enS) * min(1, dt*2.5)`.
  - Calm weight: `calm` eases to 1 when `enS < 0.3`, over ~1 s.
- **The groove** (beat = t·2.4):
  - Hips sway on the half-beat.
  - The head nods slightly behind the beat. The nod is stronger when calm.
  - The head is always cocked ~0.14 rad to the side and slowly looks around.
  - Comb lobes and wattles flop with a phase lag after the head.
  - The jaw breathes a little. The tail sways.
- **Wings:**
  - On rough water: both arms held out, slightly down, for balance. They lift a bit with energy and counter the board lean. They stay steady, with no flapping.
  - On calm water: the right wing blends into a lazy forward **shaka**, with a slow wrist-twist wiggle around the arm axis.
- **Blink:** slow and sleepy, every ~4.2 s. The lids close over ~0.5 s with a sine curve.
## 8. Surfing physics (he must surf, not fly)
- **Horizontal:**
  - He loosely circles the island at a target radius and is pushed by the water gradient.
  - Speed is capped. He is repelled from the island and bounces softly off the walls.
  - He leaves a wake (small negative disturbances behind him).
- **Vertical:**
  - Ride the surface **averaged over the board footprint**: center ×2, ±0.55 along the heading, ±0.22 across, divided by 6. This keeps single splash spikes from launching him.
  - Track the surface's vertical speed `svy`.
  - Below the surface: a firm spring, with velocity eased toward `svy`.
  - Slightly above it and not airborne: glue him to a dropping face.
  - Cap upward velocity at 2.2. In the air, use gravity ×1.8.
  - Hard clamps: never more than 0.04 below the surface and never more than **0.16 above it**. Airborne means more than 0.08 above.
  - A small splash on hard landings.
- **Board orientation:** follows the smoothed surface normal and yaws toward the direction of travel. Lean comes from lateral acceleration.
- **Target:** under extremely aggressive stirring, the median height above the surface stays ~0.01 and the maximum ≤ 0.16.
## 9. Verification
- Inspect the character in close-ups from front 3/4 (like the reference) and from the side.
  - Check that the eyes show white under the lids and the grin reads clearly.
  - Check for no visible cone-base seams on the mane and no NaN geometry warnings.
- Stress-test the waves and log the gap between the board and the averaged surface.
- Check the console for errors and keep draw calls reasonable (merge spike geometries).

title: Medieval Map Fluid Simulation and Calligraphy Story
text:
Make a short video: a hand is drawing a medieval map. Where it writes "here be dragons," the ink starts to move. The goal is to demonstrate eeriness, art direction, material truth, and sound design.

THE STORY (yours to decide)

The first act is pure craft: nib, parchment, a competent hand. Make it satisfying to watch.
The dragon is wet ink. It doesn’t have a body; it has spread, bleed, and intent. It eats towns by smearing them.
The cartographer fights with what’s on the desk: blotter, knife, sand, candle. Decide who wins, and make it a draw if you can defend it.
ART DIRECTION
Not realistic, but materially truthful: iron-gall ink, vellum grain, candle light. Calibration: Mappa Mundi; illuminated manuscript margins; ink-in-water macro photography. Limit palette to parchment, two inks, gold leaf, and one blood-red.

CHOOSE YOUR MEDIUM
The ink needs a real fluid or reaction-diffusion simulation on a 2D surface. make it as a html file, use whatever is needed

title: Tesla Roadster Collapsing Bridge Escape 3D Simulation
text:
Create a complete, single-file three.js demo (HTML + JS) that recreates the viral “Tesla Roadster flying over a collapsing bridge” concept, and make it **play automatically like a video**.

**Requirements:**

1. **Auto-play like a video**
   - The entire sequence should start automatically when the page loads (no click required to begin).
   - Cinematic camera path that follows the action smoothly from start to finish.
   - After the sequence ends, show a “Replay” button.

2. **Scene**
   - Scenic bridge over a river with forested hills in the background.
   - Clear daytime lighting with good shadows.

3. **Bridge Collapse**
   - The bridge dramatically collapses in the middle while the car is driving on it.
   - Use either physics (Cannon.js or Rapier) or a well-timed animation sequence.

4. **Car**
   - Simple but recognizable Tesla Roadster / Cybertruck-style car.
   - When the bridge starts collapsing, the car activates thrusters and flies over the gap.
   - Blue thruster glow + particle effects.
   - Smooth flight animation, then lands safely on the other side.

5. **Camera**
   - Fully cinematic, pre-scripted camera that moves for dramatic angles (starts behind the car, then shifts during the flight).
   - No free camera control during the sequence (so it feels like watching a video).

6. **Polish**
   - Clean modern three.js code (r160+).
   - “Replay” button that restarts the full sequence.
   - Responsive and runs smoothly in the browser.
   - Add basic ambient + directional lighting, fog, and a sky.

7. **Output**
   - Provide the full single HTML file I can copy and open directly in a browser.
   - Comment the important parts of the code.

Make it visually impressive and as close as possible to the concept of a flying Tesla saving itself from a collapsing bridge, while playing automatically like a short video.

# Task: Create a product promo video for "Gouo Canvas"

## Background
Gouo is my AI image platform (GitHub: zhs1234/gouo-canvas) featuring three workspaces: Image Generation, Infinite Canvas, and Creative Agent. Clone the repo and inspect src/components/landing/ (LandingPage.tsx, landing.css) and docs/zh-CN/user-guide.md before starting.

## Specs
- 16:9, 1920x1080, 30fps, ~60s, MP4 (H.264)
- No voiceover or BGM; subtle interaction SFX only

## Assets (Important)
- All generated images must use real landing preview files: public/landing/preview-{1..3}-{1..4}.webp
  - Set 1: Steak product shot
  - Set 2: Embroidered bird and flower illustration
  - Set 3: Rainy night city street
- Display real prompts verbatim; do not fabricate
- Disallow public/inspiration images and docs sketch screenshots
- Do not fake unrendered outputs (e.g. inpainting shows brush only)
- Add disclaimer text: "UI simulated · Images genuinely generated with Gouo"

## Visual Style
- Intro/Outro: Warm fluid gradient fog with film grain; title reveals from mask; floating framed cards
- Product sections: HTML re-creation of dark UI (sidebar, credits, inputs, canvas, Agent chat)
- Palette: Paper #faf8f3, Ink #171719, Accent #c26855; ease cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1)
- Progressive image reveal animation
- Glassmorphism caption card in lower-left

## Simulated Cursor
- Smooth movement, click squash with ripple, hover states, drag-and-drop targeting dynamic element positions

## Storyboard
1. Intro (0-6s): Landing hero, "From Inspiration / To Image", click CTA
2. Image Generation (6-27s): Type steak prompt, select 4 images, send, progressive reveal, favorite, launch inpainting brush
3. Infinite Canvas (27-41s): Connect text node to config node, generate 2 embroidery images, zoom out to minimap
4. Creative Agent (41-55s): Prompt agent for rainy night city, tool execution cards stream, canvas updates with new nodes
5. Outro (55-63s): Fog background, closing tagline, CTA click
Credits balance decrements accurately throughout.

## Sound Design
- Synthesized procedural SFX (subtle clicks, light typing, soft tonal chimes, breath transitions, ending chord); peak ~ -15 dBFS

## Implementation
- Single HTML page + deterministic timeline: render(t)
- Playwright frame-by-frame capture, ffmpeg encoding
- Python (numpy/scipy) audio synthesis merged into final video

title: Tesla Roadster SpaceX Rocket Launch in Three.js
text:
GOAL:
Create a highly detailed, cinematic, interactive 3D scene in Three.js where a futuristic Tesla Roadster launches from a massive rocket launch complex using reaction thrusters. The result should feel like a premium CGI spectacle with realistic materials, detailed geometry, impressive lighting, rich atmospheric effects, and smooth camera choreography.
CORE CONCEPT:
What if Tesla launched the next-generation Roadster like a SpaceX rocket? The car sits on a launch platform, secured by mechanical hold-down clamps. Warning lights flash, vapor builds, thrusters ignite, clamps release, and the Roadster rises into a controlled hover before accelerating into the sky. This is a cinematic concept, not a realistic engineering simulation.

CAR DESIGN:
Create a highly recognizable next-generation Tesla Roadster using the provided reference images. Match its silhouette, proportions, front fascia, headlights, body curves, roofline, wheels, and overall appearance as closely as possible. Use detailed geometry, premium automotive paint, realistic-looking glass, metallic materials, and convincing reflections. Avoid generic sports car shapes or overly simplistic geometry. The Roadster must remain clearly visible throughout the important stages.
LAUNCH COMPLEX:
Build a massive modern rocket launch facility with a tall launch tower, industrial gantry structures, service platforms, mechanical hold-down clamps, support arms, railings, stairs, pipes, floodlights, warning lights, vapor vents, and distant infrastructure. The environment should feel large, believable, and highly detailed. Choose a dramatic coastal, industrial, or desert setting with cinematic atmospheric lighting.

AUTOMATIC ANIMATION:
The entire sequence must start automatically when the page loads, without clicking anything. No intro screen, blank scene, or long waiting period. The first frame must already look impressive, and interesting motion should begin within the first 1–3 seconds.
ANIMATION SEQUENCE:

Hero Reveal: Begin with a cinematic shot of the Roadster on the launch platform. The camera moves smoothly while warning lights flash, vapor drifts, and industrial lighting illuminates the vehicle.
Pre-Launch: Increase atmospheric tension with smoke, pressure vents, mechanical movements, subtle vibration, and gradually intensifying thruster illumination.

Ignition: Activate the thrusters with bright exhaust, expanding smoke, particles, reflections, and lighting effects interacting with the surrounding structures.
Clamp Release: The mechanical hold-down clamps must visibly unlock, rotate, and retract away from the car. Animate their actual 3D components rather than making them disappear.

Hover: The Roadster lifts slightly above the platform and remains suspended briefly. Thrusters continue firing while smoke, dust, and lighting react beneath the vehicle. Make this moment dramatic and clearly visible.

Liftoff: The Roadster accelerates vertically past the launch tower. The camera smoothly follows the car, emphasizing scale, speed, and the power of the propulsion system.

Final Shot: Transition to a wide cinematic view showing the Roadster climbing into the sky, leaving an atmospheric exhaust trail above the launch complex.

TIMELINE:
Aim for an approximately 18–22 second cinematic sequence. Use the first 3 seconds for the hero shot and buildup, seconds 3–5 for ignition and clamp release, seconds 5–8 for hover, seconds 8–15 for ascent, and the remaining time for a dramatic final shot. Synchronize all mechanical movements, lighting changes, particles, vehicle motion, and camera animation. Use time-based animation for smooth playback.

CAMERA & LIGHTING:
Create professional cinematic camera movements, including establishing shots, slow orbits, close-ups, low-angle hero shots, hover tracking, and ascent-following shots. Keep the Roadster readable and avoid chaotic camera movements. Use dramatic sunrise, blue-hour, or nighttime lighting with industrial floodlights, realistic-looking reflections, atmospheric haze, and thruster illumination.

VISUAL EFFECTS:
Include detailed smoke plumes, pressure vapor, exhaust particles, dust, atmospheric mist, glowing thrusters, subtle heat distortion, environmental reflections, and tasteful bloom or post-processing. Effects should feel connected to the action rather than purely decorative. Smoke and lighting must react convincingly to the launch without obscuring the vehicle.

INTERACTION:
Autoplay is the priority, but optional controls may include replay, pause/resume, slow motion, camera switching, and free orbit. Keep the interface minimal and visually clean. The scene must be fully functional without any manual interaction.

TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS:
Use Three.js, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. You may use suitable open-source assets, libraries, custom shaders, particle systems, and post-processing to improve quality. Organize the project into multiple files if needed. Optimize for smooth real-time rendering and make sure it runs locally in a modern browser. This must be a real interactive 3D experience, not a prerecorded video. Test the completed scene and fix major visual or functional issues.

IMPORTANT FOR RECORDING:
The scene should be ready to record immediately after refreshing the page. Prioritize a powerful first frame, continuous animation, clearly visible mechanical movements, impressive hover and liftoff moments, and a satisfying cinematic ending. Avoid unnecessary delays or static sections.
